lessons.title: ⭐️ About Our Coaching Program
lessons.description:
We just rolled out something new for the community
→ a full coaching program where you get direct 1:1 access to specialized automation coaches
Book here → https://ea-coaching.vercel.app/
The roster covers the stuff you actually get stuck on,
→ Claude Code, ClaudeClaw OS, Cybersecurity and compliance, Make, n8n, and Sales enablement 
→ each coach has a bio so you can pick the right person for your problem
If you're on the standard monthly plan
→ you get one booking credit a month 
→ spend it, and you're back on for the next month
Premium VIP members 
→ the whole roster unlocks, and you can book my calendar at 50% off my external rate, though I'd still rather you lean on your monthly credit first
How it flows 
→ find a coach 
→ preview the booking 
→ finish the walkthrough 
→ you're connected directly 
→ manage or cancel anytime under My Sessions as long as you're outside the 13 hour window
Set your own reminders 
→ a week before, two days, two hours, one hour, whatever keeps you on time
These sessions are 𝗙𝗥𝗘𝗘 for you 
→ we pay our coaches whether you show or not, so this was never about money

→ 𝘄𝗲 𝗿𝘂𝗻 𝗮 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗸𝗲 𝗻𝗼-𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘄 𝗽𝗼𝗹𝗶𝗰𝘆

→ if you just joined and need in sooner, message me and I'll add you manually through the members tab

→ hit report a bug or reply to this post and I'll patch it fast

lessons.title: 👾 Vibe Coding Sesh: Claude Code Learning Strategy
lessons.description:
In this session, learning strategies for Claude Code usage in real engineering workflows were explored
The session covered translating meeting transcripts into scoped requirements, avoiding “one-prompt codebase” vibe-coding traps, practical use cases for sub-agents and skills, context reset strategies using GitHub issues plus parallel worktrees, database safety patterns using local Docker copies and repository boundaries
Key insights include treating AI output as code to be reviewed and refactored like any other contribution, and using small scoped tasks with frequent context resets to prevent compaction loss and cross-feature contamination

lessons.title: 🤖 AI Product Coaching Sesh:
lessons.description:
Enterprise Stack Decisions
In this session, tech stack selection tradeoffs for enterprise delivery and production-grade architecture planning were explored
The session covered cost vs DX vs reliability evaluation across Supabase/AWS/wrappers, enterprise constraints and vendor dependency risk, brief template inputs for architecture such as concurrency, background jobs, and platform scope, domain-driven design with entity/repository/service boundaries, testing priorities focused on business logic plus pragmatic manual validation
Key insights include prioritizing architecture around user concurrency and workload shape before choosing frameworks, and centralizing authentication and authorization patterns (sessions, roles, protected routes) to reduce security risk and simplify long-term maintenance

lessons.title: 👾 Vibe Coding Sesh: GitHub PR Template Workflow
lessons.description:
In this session, contributing safely to an upstream GitHub repo using forks, feature branches, and Claude Code-assisted changes were explored
The session covered forking and cloning ClaudeClaw, creating a feature branch with git checkout -b, generating issue + pull request templates via Claude Code plan/run, staging clean commits for templates vs dependency fixes, and opening a PR with a structured summary and test notes
Key insights include separating changes into logical commits for clearer review, and using PR templates to standardize summaries, test plans, and breaking-change visibility across contributors
✅ Recording bullet summary (5 lines)
🧬 Forking and cloning workflows were demonstrated for safe upstream contribution without direct writes to the source repo
🌿 Feature branching was used to isolate work (issue-template) before any changes were pushed
🧾 GitHub issue templates and a PR template were generated with Claude Code to standardize reporting and reviews
🧹 Commits were split into two clean units: template additions, then dependency/audit fixes for clearer diffs
🚀 PR creation included a tight title, change list, and testing caveats to support maintainers during review

lessons.title: 👾 Vibe Coding Sesh: GitHub PR Workflow
lessons.description:
In this session, contributing to an open-source repository with a safe GitHub fork → branch → pull request workflow were explored.
The session covered forking the ClaudeClaw repository, cloning and installing dependencies with npm, creating a feature branch for isolated changes, generating issue and pull request templates, committing changes in clean logical chunks, and opening a pull request with a clear summary and test notes.
Key insights include protecting the main branch via pull requests to reduce accidental damage, and using structured PR/issue templates plus disciplined commits to make code review faster and safer for maintainers.
—
Recording bullet summary (5)
✅ Fork-First Contribution Flow — Fork creation was used to avoid pushing changes directly to an upstream repository, followed by cloning the fork locally and verifying repository contents.
✅ Local Setup and Dependency Install — Project dependencies were installed via npm to enable local execution and validation before any remote changes.
✅ Feature Branch Isolation — A dedicated branch was created for the change set to keep work separated from default branches and simplify review/rollback.
✅ Templates for Better Collaboration — GitHub issue templates (bug + feature request) and a pull request template were added to standardize summaries, test plans, and breaking-change notes.
✅ Clean Commits and PR Creation — Changes were grouped into separate commits (templates vs dependency/security fixes), pushed to the fork branch, and submitted as a pull request with a structured change log and testing caveats.
If more recordings should be summarized the same way, paste the transcript (or upload the file) and the same 5-bullet format will be applied.

lessons.title: 👾 Vibe Coding Sesh: Claude Code Skill Install
lessons.description:

The session covered installing the Gemini API dev skill via copy/paste, resetting sessions with /clear and restarting Claude, diagnosing recurring settings/plugin errors, safely handling Gemini API keys, and using a local video file as input for skill-driven analysis
Key insights include using the simplest “copy prompt → install → restart” loop to avoid manual setup drift, and preferring transcript-based skill creation when video ingestion adds friction or timeouts

🎥 Video-to-Skill Workflow — local video input was used to trigger Gemini-powered analysis, with timeouts and long-processing expectations noted
🧠 Practical Shortcut — transcript-first skill creation was recommended for technical videos to reduce overhead and improve reliability

lessons.title: ⚙️ n8n Coaching Sech: Lead Scraping & Enrichment
lessons.description:
In this session, Mondo helps Troubleshoot a lead-gen workflow and identify better tools for scraping and enrichment.
Key Takeaways
Problem: The current workflow's core flaw is using an AI "Information Extractor" for emails, which is unreliable. It also uses Appify's Google Maps scraper, which lacks the enrichment capabilities needed for cold outreach.
Solution: Replace the current setup with Amando's "Scrape Google Maps & Enrich with AI" flow from Skool. This flow uses Bright Data's MCP client for reliable web scraping and an AI agent for accurate, custom enrichment (e.g., finding owners).
Tooling: Use AnyMailFinder for verified email discovery. For custom sites like a Chamber of Commerce directory, use Bright Data's MCP client, not a browser-based tool, as it's designed for scraping, not interaction.
Cost: Bright Data's MCP client is pay-per-use at ~$1.05 per 1,000 results. Appify's $39/mo plan provides $39 in usage credits.Current Workflow Analysis
Goal: Scrape leads from Google Maps for cold outreach.
Process: Form Submission → Appify HTTP Request → Filter → AI "Information Extractor" → Validate → Append to Excel.
Flaws Identified:
Email Discovery: The "Information Extractor" is unreliable for finding and validating emails.
Enrichment: The workflow lacks a robust method to enrich data with custom fields (e.g., contact names, job titles) for personalized outreach.
Efficiency: The initial filter for websites is redundant, as Appify's Google Maps scraper can be configured to return only businesses with websites.

lessons.title: 👾 Vibe Coding Sesh: Database Schema for MVP
lessons.description:
What This Meeting Was About
We refined the blueprint for how an AI travel planner stores and organizes its data — making sure claude code is only building what's needed for the first version of the product.

---
Key Takeaways
1. You have to tell Claude Code exactly what role to play. Some AI tools come with built-in guidance on how to manage a project. Claude Code doesn't — you need to explicitly prompt it to think like a product manager, helping you define what to build first and what to save for later.
2. The first version should only do one thing well. We stripped out everything that wasn't essential to the core experience: a user fills out a questionnaire, and the AI generates a personalized itinerary. Features like tracking where leads come from or managing sales contacts were pushed to version two.
3. The data structure should mirror what the user actually sees and does. If the user isn't typing something into the app in version one, there's no reason to build a place to store it in the database. This keeps development lean and focused.
4. Supabase is our database platform. Think of Supabase as the filing cabinet where all user and itinerary data lives. We updated our blueprint to match this specific tool since that's what we're building on.

---
The Problem We Solved
The AI over-built the blueprint. When we first asked Claude Code to design the data structure, it created storage for features we don't need yet — things like lead tracking, sales rep assignments, and advanced reporting. That's like furnishing rooms in a house you haven't built yet. It wastes time and delays launch.
How we fixed it — step by step:
We walked Claude Code through four rounds of refinement, each one trimming the blueprint closer to what version one actually needs.
Round 1 – Switch the platform. We told it to redesign the blueprint for Supabase, our chosen tool.
Round 2 – Cut unnecessary sections. We told it we're only building version one, so remove anything that isn't core to the product. It eliminated eight entire sections of the blueprint that were earmarked for future features.
Round 3 – Cut unnecessary details within sections. Even after removing whole sections, some remaining ones still had fields related to marketing and lead tracking baked in. We told it to strip those out too.
Round 4 – Match the blueprint to the actual user experience. We reviewed what the questionnaire actually asks the user and found the blueprint still included data fields the user never fills out. We listed those specifically and had Claude Code remove them.

When we first asked Claude Code to design the data structure, it created storage for features we don't need yet — things like lead tracking, sales rep assignments, and advanced reporting. That's like furnishing rooms in a house you haven't built yet. It wastes time and delays launch.
How we fixed it — step by step:
We walked Claude Code through four rounds of refinement, each one trimming the blueprint closer to what version one actually needs.
Round 1 – Switch the platform.
We told it to redesign the blueprint for Supabase, our chosen tool.
Round 2 – Cut unnecessary sections.
We told it we're only building version one, so remove anything that isn't core to the product. It eliminated eight entire sections of the blueprint that were earmarked for future features.
Round 3 – Cut unnecessary details within sections.
Even after removing whole sections, some remaining ones still had fields related to marketing and lead tracking baked in. We told it to strip those out too.
Round 4 – Match the blueprint to the actual user experience.
We reviewed what the questionnaire actually asks the user and found the blueprint still included data fields the user never fills out. We listed those specifically and had Claude Code remove them.

lessons.title: ⚙️🆕 n8n Coaching Sesh: Multiple n8n to Claude
lessons.description:
Meeting Purpose
Connect Karen's N8N instances to Claude using Smithery MCP so she can use Claude as an active co-pilot inside her automation workflows.

---
Context
The Problem: Karen's existing Claude ↔ N8N connection had broken, leaving her without AI assistance inside her workflows. She also wanted to connect a second N8N instance (her client's).
The Tool: Smithery is a platform that hosts MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers — it acts as a bridge that allows Claude to read and interact with external tools like N8N directly.
The Environment: Karen is on Windows, which introduced some installation friction that required a workaround during setup.
End Goal: Have both Karen's personal N8N instance and her client's N8N instance connected to Claude, enabling her to build and manage workflows conversationally.
---
Topics
1. Installing Node.js on Windows
Why it's needed: Smithery's CLI installation command runs through NPX, which requires Node.js to be installed on the machine.
What happened: Running the Smithery install command in the Command Prompt failed because Node was not installed.
Fix:
Search for "install Node.js" in Google
Download the Windows 64-bit installer from nodejs.org
Run the installer, then close and reopen the Command Prompt to refresh the environment
Key takeaway: Always restart your terminal after installing Node so the system recognizes the new installation.
---
2. Smithery CLI Troubleshooting on Windows
What happened: Even after installing Node, the Smithery install command returned a crash error (fetch failed, type error).
Root cause: Likely a Windows-specific compatibility issue with Smithery's CLI installer.
Workaround used: Instead of installing via the terminal, the MCP server URL was copied directly from Smithery and added manually into Claude as a Custom Connector.
Key takeaway: When a CLI install fails, Smithery allows you to add MCP servers manually through Claude's connector settings — this is a reliable fallback on Windows.
---
3. Connecting a Client's N8N Instance to Claude
Path: Claude → Customize → Connectors → + → Add Custom Connector → Paste Remote MCP Server URL
Steps walkthrough:
Go to Smithery, search for N8N Workflow Builder, and copy the MCP server URL
In Claude, go to Customize → Connectors → Add Custom Connector
Paste the URL, remove any trailing backslash
Go to the client's N8N instance → Settings → N8N API → Create API Key (label it "Claude")
Copy the API key and paste it into the connector setup, then hit Connect
Result: Claude successfully connected to the client's N8N instance ✅
---
4. The MCP-Available Trigger Requirement
Discovery: Not all workflow triggers in N8N are visible or accessible through the MCP connection. Only specific trigger types qualify.
MCP-compatible triggers:
Webhook Trigger
Form Trigger
Chat Trigger
Scheduled Trigger
Practical fix: If a workflow uses a trigger type outside this list (e.g., Google Drive trigger), add a Form Trigger node as well, then publish the workflow. This satisfies the MCP requirement without breaking the original logic.
Key takeaway: For Claude to interact with a workflow via MCP, the workflow must be published and contain at least one MCP-compatible trigger.
---
5. Verifying the Connection Works
Test used: Asked Claude to read a specific workflow by its ID (found in the URL of the workflow editor, after /workflow/)
Permission best practices introduced:
Allow Once → Use for any creation or modification actions
Always Allow → Use for any read-only actions
Result: Claude successfully retrieved and read the workflow, confirming the MCP connection was live ✅
---
6. Connecting Karen's Personal N8N Instance
Repeated the same Custom Connector setup for Karen's own N8N instance
Generated a new API key from her personal N8N settings and connected it the same way
Result: Both instances — Karen's personal and her client's — are now fully connected to Claude ✅
---
Key Takeaways for the Student
Smithery:A platform to host and deploy MCP servers that connect Claude to external tools

lessons.title: 1) Why Most AI Consultants Will Fail 📉
lessons.description:
Your positioning determines your price -- and your survival rate
20 minutes on why saying "no" to clients makes you more money than saying "yes" to everyone, and the framework that's survived 2,000+ hours across companies you'd recognize
What you'll watch:
The "Yes you're all wrong" positioning strategy
Four readiness checkpoints that determine if someone can even use AI
Three-tier pricing model (Implementation → Prep → Education)
Why refunding clients gets you more businessThe core positioning shift:
Don't give clients what they WANT (newest tools, all the features, DevDay highlights)
Give them what they NEED (readiness assessment, process fixes, honest limits)
The provocative statement to steal:
"AI is a luxury, not a right. You earn the ability to use AI. You don't just get it."
The Four Readiness Checkpoints:
Before selling ANY implementation, ask:
Processes: Do they exist? Documented? If not, you're building on a garbage truck on fire
Data: Where does it live? SQL? Do they have a data dictionary? (Litmus test for maturity)
Buy-in: C-suite on board or Trojan horse situation? Wrong management = 40% failure rate
Systems: Built automations before? Speak Make/N8N? Different hemisphere entirelyIf they fail 2+ checkpoints? Don't sell implementation. Sell readiness.The Three-Tier Strategy Framework:
Tier 1 - Implementation (they're ready):
Build automations or consult so well they let you build
$200/month retainer to stay embeddedTier 2 - Prep (not ready):
Organize their processes first
Fix the foundation before adding AI
This is where you make the most money 👈Tier 3 - Education (need training):
ChatGPT/Claude workshops (still the best seller)
Train on fixing organizational problemsCritical lessons from 2,000+ hours:
Short-term vs long-term tradeoff:
- Hype positioning: More clients faster, more churn, temporal income
- Honest positioning: Fewer clients, zero churn, premium prices, referral machine
Real example: "I've refunded consults when clients push me toward solutions I don't believe in. Every time I do this, I get MORE business."
The consulting arbitrage window:
6-12 months before AI can teach better than us. Use this time to:
Do free 15-min consults if starting at zero
Rack up dozens of calls
Build pattern recognition across industriesCommon consulting pitfalls:
Being the Trojan horse (hired by non-C-suite, hated by leadership)
The $5K/month subscription audit that saves $3K (builds trust for $30-40K engagements)
Teaching tools to companies with no processes
Over-indexing on one tool (voice only, chat only, Claude only)The buy-in technique for hostile rooms:
"Let me show you three types of people. Jim (burning down ChatGPT) - some of you hate that I exist. I come in peace. I'm skeptical too, which is why [stakeholder] trusted me."
Call it out. Acknowledge it. Move forward.Why generalist knowledge matters:
Companies need:
Systems that share the same brain
Tools outside their database to avoid technical debt
Multiple automation layers
Someone who understands the full spectrum"We're going to crush huge consulting firms because they're bloated, not nimble, and their consultants watch our videos to make their decks."
The positioning that wins: ✅
Not: "Here's everything from OpenAI DevDay and how to use it all"
But: "Here's what matters for YOUR situation, and here's why 90% of that doesn't apply to you yet"
Result: Premium pricing, clients that stay for years, referrals that pre-qualify themselves.Pin https://www.skool.com/earlyaidopters/consulting-playbook-day-1-why-most-ai-consultants-will-fail?p=95bea32c

lessons.title: 2) The Art of the Discovery Call (P1)
lessons.description:
Be an AI doctor, not an AI drug dealer.
How to diagnose client readiness, ask the right scope questions, and identify red flags before you waste time building solutions on broken foundations.
What you'll watch:
The opening framework that positions you as the expert
Three critical scope questions (Scale → Stack → Knowledge)
How to map their entire tech ecosystem in real-time
Red flags that mean "don't take this client yet"The core philosophy shift:
AI Doctor: Diagnose → Provide prognosis → Prescribe what they actually need
AI Drug Dealer: Hear pain point → Immediately pitch your sexiest solution
"Drug dealers are profitable in the short term. Doctors build trust and are profitable long-term."
Opening the call:
When they ask "How do you usually run these things?"
Your answer: "My goal is to fix your pain point or help you reach your goal. I already read your Calendly notes and briefed myself on your company. I'd love to hear in your own words: what are the day-to-day pain points you, your team, and your company are dealing with?"
This immediately positions you as:
Prepared (you did your homework)
Focused on their problems (not your solutions)
Diagnostic (listening before prescribing)Critical paid call rule:
If someone spends 10 minutes explaining their pain point, extend the call by 10 minutes. Those were venting minutes, not solutioning minutes. Don't nickel and dime people. Build long-term relationships.
The Three Scope Questions:
Question 1 - SCALE (How many employees?)
Pattern matching by company size:
5-20: Flat hierarchy, minimal processes
21-50: Policies start appearing, first managers
51-100: Series B/C territory, real structure
100-500: Defined departments, politics emerge
500-1,000: Could be public, series D/E
1,000-5,000: Enterprise tier
10,000+: Full enterprise, maximum bureaucracy🧠 Pro tip: VC-backed startups (50-100 employees) usually have budget set aside by investors for efficiency improvements. They're AI-first, AI-leading, very open to investing.
Bootstrapped vs VC-backed changes everything about budget availability and speed of decision-making.Question 2 - STACK (What tools do you use day-to-day?)
While they're talking, run Perplexity searches in the background:
"Does [tool name] have an API endpoint open to developers?"
If no API: Can we migrate? How important is this tool?
If locked in: Note this as a constraint for laterReal-time pattern recognition:
"We use Google Drive, Notion, Slack"
→ Google ecosystem, easier integrations, straightforward automations
"We use Outlook, OneDrive, Microsoft Teams"
→ Microsoft ecosystem, often public sector/non-profit, OneDrive permissions are devastating, need internal IT help
The stack categories to map:
Comms: Slack vs Teams vs Discord
Docs/Knowledge: Google Drive vs OneDrive vs Dropbox vs Notion
CRM: HubSpot vs Salesforce vs Pipedrive (and how well is it configured?)
Project Management: Monday vs Asana vs ClickUp (does it have an API?)
Data/BI: Power BI vs Tableau vs Looker vs Google Sheets Empire
Design: Figma vs Canva
Dev Tools: GitHub vs Bitbucket vs private repos
Database: Supabase vs Firebase vs Convex
Meeting Notes: Fathom vs Gong vs Fireflies (each has different integration capabilities)Critical discovery about CRMs:
"These systems are only as good as the people who set them up and the hygiene in which they use the tool."
Real example: Sales team using HubSpot, but campaigns are named "001_week", "001_week(1)", "001_week(2)"
Result: You accept the contract, get the milestone payment, dive into their system, and realize it's way more work than expected. Now they think you understand the assignment, but you barely understand what's involved.
Question 3 - KNOWLEDGE (Where does your data live?)
Three possible answers:
One central repository (rare, ideal)
Scattered but organized
Completely disparate and scattered 🚨If answer is #3:
"The first exercise will NOT be an automation. It will NOT be a vibe-coded app. The first exercise is getting your stuff in order so you're eligible to even benefit from AI."
The doctor's diagnosis framework:
What they present with:
Use AI individually, no integrations
Scattered knowledge across platforms
Overwhelmed by options
Want to "AI-ify everything"
Spending days on LinkedIn**Pin: https://www.skool.com/earlyaidopters/consulting-playbook-day-2-the-art-of-the-discovery-call-p1?p=df8968fc

Comms: Slack vs Teams vs Discord
Docs/Knowledge: Google Drive vs OneDrive vs Dropbox vs Notion
CRM: HubSpot vs Salesforce vs Pipedrive (and how well is it configured?)
Project Management: Monday vs Asana vs ClickUp (does it have an API?)
Data/BI: Power BI vs Tableau vs Looker vs Google Sheets Empire
Design: Figma vs Canva
Dev Tools: GitHub vs Bitbucket vs private repos
Database: Supabase vs Firebase vs Convex
Meeting Notes: Fathom vs Gong vs Fireflies (each has different integration capabilities)
Critical discovery about CRMs:
"These systems are only as good as the people who set them up and the hygiene in which they use the tool."
Real example:
Sales team using HubSpot, but campaigns are named "001_week", "001_week(1)", "001_week(2)"
Result:

You accept the contract, get the milestone payment, dive into their system, and realize it's way more work than expected. Now they think you understand the assignment, but you barely understand what's involved.
Question 3 - KNOWLEDGE (Where does your data live?)
Three possible answers:
One central repository (rare, ideal)
Scattered but organized
Completely disparate and scattered 🚨
If answer is #3:
"The first exercise will NOT be an automation. It will NOT be a vibe-coded app. The first exercise is getting your stuff in order so you're eligible to even benefit from AI."
The doctor's diagnosis framework:
What they present with:
Use AI individually, no integrations
Scattered knowledge across platforms
Overwhelmed by options
Want to "AI-ify everything"
Spending days on LinkedIn

lessons.title: 3) Reading the Room & Red Flags 🚩
lessons.description:
How to diagnose three client scenarios and when to pump the brakes
24 minutes on pattern matching by company type, the recommendation framework that prevents scope creep, and the red flags that scream "this client will be a nightmare."
What you'll watch:
Three company archetypes and what each one actually needs
The platform prescription framework (ChatGPT vs Claude vs Gemini vs Custom)
Blue sky scenario sessions that unlock hidden use cases
Red flags 🚩 that mean pump the brakes immediatelyThe core problem this solves:
Discovery calls fail because of noise on both sides:
You're rambling, adding too much context
They're confused, pivoting left/right/center
The message gets lost in translationGoal: Bridge the gap when articulation fails on one side and digestion fails on the other.
Scenario A - Small Team (5-20 people)
The setup:
Everyone uses free ChatGPT
Real startup, broke, maybe bootstrapped
Core tools: Gmail, Notion, Slack
Budget: $500-$2K/month (including your fee)
Needs: Simple setup, quick wins, low overheadThe diagnosis:
If max budget is $2K and ChatGPT Teams is $25/person:
20 people × $25 = $500/month (25% of budget)
If they're risk-averse and only spend $1K, that's 50% of their AI budgetCan you do everything with just ChatGPT? Yes.
Why: Gmail, Notion, Slack all have MCP servers/connectors → Everything can route through ChatGPT Teams → Add agent builder, custom GPTs, projects, workflows → They're set.
Your prescription: "Just pay for ChatGPT Teams. Higher security than free version. You can connect to any API with custom schemas if there's no native connector."
This team needs ONE tool done right, not 15 tools done poorly.
Scenario B - Mid-Size (21-100 people)
The setup:
10-15 paid AI tools
Using each tool only 20% of potential
Tools conflict (didn't know ChatGPT does images like Midjourney)
Knowledge in multiple places
Budget: $2K-$10K/month
Needs: Phased rollouts, department focus, integration priorityThe diagnosis:
Not broke. Not lacking resources. Lacking direction.
Your goal here: Small retainer to keep your foot in the door ($200-500/month)
Why: You stay embedded → Trusted advisor position → When workshop/roadmap opportunity comes up, you're already there
The phased rollout strategy:
Start with 10 power users (revenue-adjacent roles)
Run a pilot for 2-3 weeks
Get scattered data into central repo (Google Drive/Dropbox/OneDrive)
Cut 15 tools down to 5 (or even 3)The secret weapon: Claude Code
"I don't care if you're not developers. I don't care if you're afraid of the terminal. This is your Swiss Army knife for building anything at scale."
Focus on sales/revenue-adjacent departments first.
Why: If they report to a board, they need tangible return on initial value (not ROI, but first taste of what's possible) → More budget gets unlocked → Skeptics start paying attention
The Blue Sky Scenario Session:
After 2-3 weeks of pilot success:
Bring in people who experienced the first "aha moment"
Ask: "Now that you know a sliver of what's possible, what would change your day-to-day? How could you become 10x more efficient? In a perfect world where AI didn't hallucinate, was affordable, what would you want to accomplish?"
Will you grant 90% of these wishes? No.
But you'll hear ideas from people who wouldn't otherwise speak up.
Take those ideas → Run them through RICE scoring framework:
- Reach: How many people affected?
- Impact: What gets solved?
- Confidence: Out of 100, can you actually build this?
- Effort: How much work required?
Use this to prioritize the blue sky ideas systematically.
Scenario C - Enterprise (100+ people)
The setup:
- Many systems (Workday, Greenhouse, Salesforce, HubSpot, Zoho - 8 systems where 1 would satisfy a normal company)
- Heavily siloed knowledge
- Complex approval processes, bureaucracy, red tape
- Needs: Pilot programs, security reviews, change management
The brutal reality:
6-12 months to fix their system architecture → That's long-term, not immediate win
These enterprises need to LOOK like they're embracing AI (public/private shareholders) → They need shiny things that work NOW
Your hack: Build something that lives OUTSIDE their spaghetti back-end mess
Example use case: Knowledge sharing tool for 522 product SKUs
Vibe code something immediately accessible by dozens of users → One central knowledge repo → User research to populate it → Shows the org what "moving quick" looks like
Why you care about moving quick: Break down red tape ideologies, resistance to change, inspire them to throw resources at manifesting the AI dream
Enterprise warning: Never the same content twice. Each situation has unique political factors, EU regulations, medical constraints, controversial products, etc.
The Recommendation Framework:
Step 1 - Choose the platform (match requirements to tools)
ChatGPT when:
Need broad integrations
Google Workspace heavy
Team collaboration required
Want image generation + voice features
Want one ecosystem (plus fine-tuning, assistants, agent builder)Claude when:
Deep reasoning required
Complex analysis needed
Document-heavy workflows (unless docs are too large)
Research tasksGemini when:
Google ecosystem locked in
Video input required
YouTube integration needed
Cost-sensitive (very gracious free rate limits)Custom Build when:
Enterprise with resources
Blue sky scenario made it obvious
Production-level code deployed on cloud provider (not vibe-coded app)
This is enterprise play onlyStep 2 - Explain the trade-offs
Make it abundantly clear: "Your recommendation comes with sacrifice."
Example: They love Gamma's yellow/blue design. Claude's PowerPoints look more dry.
These are touchy-feely things you need to rip off like a bandaid.
Be politely savage: "Like a personal trainer, being nice when you're 100 pounds over your weight loss goal won't help. You need to cut refined carbs and hit the weights 5× a week."
The honest advisor play:
"I could charge you hourly and you'd need me for 6 months. I could accumulate billables. But I want to sleep at night knowing I gave you highest information density per minute. I want to get you there in as few steps as possible."
Step 3 - Create Plan B (the redundancy plan)
Every organization has its own heartbeat → Plan A might not work
Plan A roadmap: 30/60/90/180/365 days
Plan B: If you get crazy C-suite pushback or Luddites poison-pill the company
Backup options:
Open source models?
Self-hosted N8N instances?
No licenses needed if someone blocks subscriptions?Real talk: "I've been on calls with 10 people who hate my existence just because I'm trying to help them embrace AI. You won't always be seen as the hero. Sometimes you're the villain." 👀
Common pitfalls to warn them about:
Don't chase features
Don't overbuild (don't use 10 agents because YouTube made it look sexy)
Don't skip foundations
Don't rush rollouts
Don't ignore training (upsell opportunity for workshops)
Don't forget security (some companies will streak naked with customer data)Build philosophy:
Simple > Sophisticated
Build 80% first, worry about 20% later
Foundational > Flashy (unless you need quick win for political reasons)
In-house > Agency (business requirements change constantly)RED FLAGS - When to Pump the Brakes: 🚨
"We need AI agents NOW"
→ No you don't. You need to get your grip together. Even in best workflows, AI agents are used once or twice max. Determinism is the best way to build workflows.
"I saw this on LinkedIn"
→ Scope creep superhero. Red flag incarnate.
"My competitor has it"
→ You're building AI for wrong reasons. Different companies, different heartbeats, different bureaucracy. What works for them won't work for you.
"It MUST be cutting-edge"
→ Cutting edge = bleeding edge = high risk of bugs, landscape changes, technology shifts. Don't build enterprise-scale on something that came out last week.
When you see multiple red flags: Pump the brakes. These clients will be more headache than blessing.
The future-proof recommendation:
"Here's the minimum stack this organization needs. No matter what Gemini or Anthropic releases next month, stick to this. Even if it looks like you're behind for one month, next month you might have the leading model. Once this permeates through your team's lens of AI, you'll be the trusted advisor."
Next episode: Solution design - how to architect AI implementations that actually stick

lessons.title: 4) Solution Design & Pricing That Scales
lessons.description:
From chaos to systematic execution 🦾
23 minutes on mapping current state, building KPI frameworks that justify your work, and the pricing tier strategy that keeps clients in your ecosystem forever.
What you'll watch:
The 4-part current state mapping framework (tools, knowledge, processes, owners)
Baseline metrics that prove ROI before and after
Pilot → Scale → Optimize rollout structure
Pricing tiers from $10/month community to $15K+ enterprise
The 60-minute call structure that closes dealsThe confidence principle:
"The more systematic you are, the more they derive confidence from YOUR confidence about the process."
Even if they're not 100% sure how well you'll do, a solid systematized plan gives them confidence to move forward.
Part 1 - Current State Mapping (The Murder Mystery Framework)
Think of this like a murder mystery dinner: Someone murdered time. Someone murdered efficiency. Your job: Find out who, what, when, and why.
Worksheet 1 - Map All Current Tools:
Columns you need:
Tool/Platform Name
Type of Tool (AI or non-AI)
Use Case (why they're using it)
Department
Number of UsersWhy number of users matters: "If we do this first, it will affect 500 users. That's a third of your company." → Gives you ammo for prioritization.Worksheet 2 - Find Knowledge Sources:
Map every single knowledge source:
Notion, Slack docs, Confluence, Jira, internal wikis
Type of document
Connected AI tools (including quick and dirty RAG setups)
Where it's stored
How often it's updated (critical for RAG viability)
Size and volumeThe RAG decision questions (always ask these):
"What data types? PDF, doc, image, video?"
"How big? How many?"
This tells you: Can we dump this in a large context window, or do you need proper RAG? If RAG, what level? Quick and dirty? Hybrid RAG? Agentic RAG (10,000 pages → 100 page cheat sheet)?Worksheet 3 - Document Processes:
Spend 1-2 hours mapping:
Decision points
Operational procedures
Tacit knowledge they forget to mention⚠️ Warning: Even if they think they understand their own process, once you get into solutioning, tacit knowledge gaps will appear. This worksheet gives you a starting point.Worksheet 4 - Identify the Owners (The Suspects):
Map who owns what:
Business owners of each tool/process
Technical owners (many companies have zero)
Who holds the money (CFO? Controller? C-suite?)Why this matters:
Solutioning requires knowing the budget
Understanding political allegiances ("Do you like Gamma because you've used it for 2 years, even though Claude 4.5 Sonnet now does the same thing?")
Knowing who to contact for specific decisionsPart 2 - Baseline Assessment (Prove Your Value)
"Otherwise people will say we spoke to an AI consultant and accomplished nothing because you couldn't make it tangible."
Metrics that matter.Before/After measurements:
Time spent on manual tasks
Error rates on processes (50 out of 100 applications are edge cases)
Cost per transaction/output
Employee satisfaction score
Customer satisfaction metrics (if client-facing)Target outcomes:
% reduction in manual processing time
Accuracy improvement targets
ROI and cost saving goals
User adoption rate targets
Output quality improvementsThe KPI framework structure:
For each metric, document:
KPI name
Baseline value
Target value
Measurement method
Review frequencyReview frequency nuance: Don't measure day-by-day. Fridays = less productive. Mondays = less productive. Humans are humans. Weekly or monthly is better.
"The numbers are here as anchors for you. When you're grilled by C-suite, this is what you hold onto."Part 3 - Implementation Rollout Strategy
Phase 1 - PILOT (30-60 days):
Select pilot group (count on one hand how many people)
Train core users
Run for 30-60 days
Collect feedback
Analyze results
Document wins in metric format (tangible reporting)
Document issues
Refine processes (assumed people always do X, Y, Z → turns out only 60% of the time)Adherence metric: "What % of people doing X continue doing X every Y frequency?"
Phase 2 - SCALE:
Train next cohort (much bigger group)
Deploy to entire department
Monitor adoption and adherence
Track metrics from pilot issuesPhase 3 - OPTIMIZE (3-6-12 months):
Expand gradually across organization.
Reality check: Some departments don't need AI for a while. Some are so messy with technical debt it's not worth expanding until you have proven momentum.
Goals:
Track KPIs
Identify bottlenecks (they keep popping up)
Stay on top of model changes (3.5 Turbo deprecated mid-2026)
Critical gaps identified
Recommended next steps"As models change and deprecate, bottlenecks will continue. Your responsibility: Either YOU monitor this, or give the organization what they need to do it themselves."
Part 4 - Centralized Strategy Checklist
Before implementation, know:
Where SOPs, customer data, company knowledge lives
Tool structure (using MCP servers? Which ones and why?)
If they use Zapier for 90% of things, does it make sense to say "switch to N8N" just because you prefer it?
Assess connectors, custom APIs, etc.Department priorities for pilots:
Revenue-adjacent = highest value. Even 1% incremental positive change = tangible benefit = wind under your sails.
1. Sales use cases:
Lead research
Email drafting
CRM updates
Qualification
Follow-up sequences
Meeting prep2. Support use cases:
Ticket summarization
Response templates
Knowledge search
Escalation routing
Customer history
Auto-drafting replies (with human-in-the-loop approval)Real example: E-commerce getting hundreds of tickets/day. Low-level informational tickets = autonomous response. Edge cases ("I ordered in Slovenia, now in Australia") = human intervention.3. Marketing use cases:
Content creation
SEO research (very popular now)
Social posting
Ad copy
Campaign analysis4. Operations use cases:
Process documentation
Data cleanup
Report automation
Workflow optimizationPart 5 - Engagement Options & Pricing Tiers
The community downsell hack:
Instead of losing clients after 1-2 paid calls, create a mini-community (5-10 people):
"You don't have to pay $150/$500/$1000 for another 2-hour call. Get fractionalized access to me. I'll answer everyone's questions once a week in this community."
Could be on School, Circle, wherever. Price: $10-20/month.
Goal: Your foot stays in the door with people who otherwise wouldn't book another call.
Tight Budget Tier:
$10-20/month community
Your foot in the door
Even if starting out, fractionalized access beats nothingMedium Budget Tier:
$250-500 per call
Prepare beforehand (don't get informed minutes before)
Minute 1 after weather talk = straight to value
Bundle: Pay per session + answer X emails associated with the call
Most popular: 15-minute calls (15 min prep, decent ROI)Real Budget Tier (Retainer):
$2K-10K/month
Weekly check-ins
Ongoing support by email (use templates so they don't send Hobbit essays)
Small builds: GPTs, projects, automations you can repurpose
Team training, priority access
Bundles increase valueTemplate for decision point emails:
"When you send me a question about a decision point, frame it like: Problem, What You've Tried, Question."
Makes it easier for you to answer without syncing every time.
Enterprise Tier:
$15K+ project-based
Full implementation
Multi-department engagements
Subcontract developers to extend LTV and average order value
Ongoing change management
Public sector = way more expensive (nice numbers, but red tape/bureaucracy/audits)"Instead of the Big Four getting it, why don't you get it?"
How to frame options when budget is unknown:
"I have three ways we can work together:
Most affordable: $20/month community
Middle ground: 30-minute or 15-minute call
Premium: Package of 4 one-hour calls for $1200"Let them choose. Don't push. Having tiers increases likelihood of working together.
The brutal truth about knowledge vs relationships:
"In the next 12-18 months, all knowledge for knowledge's sake will be worthless. Relationships will be paramount."
Don't nickel and dime, but balance it. Don't be taken advantage of where they pay way less than the value you give in time spent.
Real example: Got email from former client about decision point. Two-sentence answer, one minute of thinking → Didn't charge. Pro relationship over nickel and diming.
Part 6 - Be The Calm In The Chaos
"When you converse with a client, be the person they come to for calmness, not agitation or friction."
Most people in this space = overwhelmed and lost (deservedly so).
Phrases to use:
"Ignore the noise"
"Start simple"
"You're not behind"
"We'll build this correctly together"Position yourself as a PARTNER, not a dollar sign relationship.
Always have a next step before next session:
Examples:
List all the tools you have
Map all data locations
Define three use cases
Get budget approval (could take multiple sessions)
Pick pilot department
Assign a championThe 60-Minute Call Structure:
0-5 min: Pain and goal
5-15 min: Real discovery
15-25 min: Diagnosing
25-35 min: Recommendation (walk through why it might not be realistic for their business)
35-40 min: Next stepsCall checklist:
- Start with pain/goal
- Ask scale questions
- Map their stack (mentally if you think in workflows)
- Find knowledge gaps
- Give HONEST advice
- Warn of pitfalls
- Show alternatives (different ways to solve same thing, which are quicker/cheaper)
- Offer pricing tiers"The more reps you get in, the more readily available this information will be for you."

Metrics that matter.
Before/After measurements:
Time spent on manual tasks
Error rates on processes (50 out of 100 applications are edge cases)
Cost per transaction/output
Employee satisfaction score
Customer satisfaction metrics (if client-facing)
Target outcomes:
% reduction in manual processing time
Accuracy improvement targets
ROI and cost saving goals
User adoption rate targets
Output quality improvements
The KPI framework structure:
For each metric, document:
KPI name
Baseline value
Target value
Measurement method
Review frequency
Review frequency nuance: Don't measure day-by-day. Fridays = less productive. Mondays = less productive. Humans are humans. Weekly or monthly is better.
"The numbers are here as anchors for you. When you're grilled by C-suite, this is what you hold onto."
Part 3 - Implementation Rollout Strategy
Phase 1 - PILOT (30-60 days):
Select pilot group (count on one hand how many people)
Train core users
Run for 30-60 days
Collect feedback
Analyze results
Document wins in metric format (tangible reporting)
Document issues
Refine processes (assumed people always do X, Y, Z → turns out only 60% of the time)
Adherence metric: "What % of people doing X continue doing X every Y frequency?"
Phase 2 - SCALE:
Train next cohort (much bigger group)
Deploy to entire department
Monitor adoption and adherence
Track metrics from pilot issues
Phase 3 - OPTIMIZE (3-6-12 months):
Expand gradually across organization.
Reality check: Some departments don't need AI for a while. Some are so messy with technical debt it's not worth expanding until you have proven momentum.
Goals:
Track KPIs
Identify bottlenecks (they keep popping up)
Stay on top of model changes (3.5 Turbo deprecated mid-2026)
Critical gaps identified
Recommended next steps
"As models change and deprecate, bottlenecks will continue. Your responsibility: Either YOU monitor this, or give the organization what they need to do it themselves."
Part 4 - Centralized Strategy Checklist
Before implementation, know:
Where SOPs, customer data, company knowledge lives
Tool structure (using MCP servers? Which ones and why?)
If they use Zapier for 90% of things, does it make sense to say "switch to N8N" just because you prefer it?
Assess connectors, custom APIs, etc.
Department priorities for pilots:
Revenue-adjacent = highest value. Even 1% incremental positive change = tangible benefit = wind under your sails.
1. Sales use cases:
Lead research
Email drafting
CRM updates
Qualification
Follow-up sequences
Meeting prep
2. Support use cases:
Ticket summarization
Response templates
Knowledge search
Escalation routing
Customer history
Auto-drafting replies (with human-in-the-loop approval)
Real example:
E-commerce getting hundreds of tickets/day. Low-level informational tickets = autonomous response. Edge cases ("I ordered in Slovenia, now in Australia") = human intervention.
3. Marketing use cases:
Content creation
SEO research (very popular now)
Social posting
Ad copy
Campaign analysis
4. Operations use cases:
Process documentation
Data cleanup
Report automation
Workflow optimization
Part 5 - Engagement Options & Pricing Tiers
The community downsell hack:
Instead of losing clients after 1-2 paid calls, create a mini-community (5-10 people):
"You don't have to pay $150/$500/$1000 for another 2-hour call. Get fractionalized access to me. I'll answer everyone's questions once a week in this community."
Could be on School, Circle, wherever. Price: $10-20/month.
Goal: Your foot stays in the door with people who otherwise wouldn't book another call.
Tight Budget Tier:
$10-20/month community
Your foot in the door
Even if starting out, fractionalized access beats nothing
Medium Budget Tier:
$250-500 per call
Prepare beforehand (don't get informed minutes before)
Minute 1 after weather talk = straight to value
Bundle: Pay per session + answer X emails associated with the call
Most popular: 15-minute calls (15 min prep, decent ROI)
Real Budget Tier (Retainer):
$2K-10K/month
Weekly check-ins
Ongoing support by email (use templates so they don't send Hobbit essays)
Small builds: GPTs, projects, automations you can repurpose
Team training, priority access
Bundles increase value
Template for decision point emails:
"When you send me a question about a decision point, frame it like: Problem, What You've Tried, Question."
Makes it easier for you to answer without syncing every time.
Enterprise Tier:
$15K+ project-based
Full implementation
Multi-department engagements
Subcontract developers to extend LTV and average order value
Ongoing change management
Public sector = way more expensive (nice numbers, but red tape/bureaucracy/audits)
"Instead of the Big Four getting it, why don't you get it?"
How to frame options when budget is unknown:
"I have three ways we can work together:
Most affordable: $20/month community
Middle ground: 30-minute or 15-minute call
Premium: Package of 4 one-hour calls for $1200"
Let them choose. Don't push. Having tiers increases likelihood of working together.
The brutal truth about knowledge vs relationships:
"In the next 12-18 months, all knowledge for knowledge's sake will be worthless. Relationships will be paramount."
Don't nickel and dime, but balance it. Don't be taken advantage of where they pay way less than the value you give in time spent.
Real example: Got email from former client about decision point. Two-sentence answer, one minute of thinking → Didn't charge. Pro relationship over nickel and diming.
Part 6 - Be The Calm In The Chaos
"When you converse with a client, be the person they come to for calmness, not agitation or friction."
Most people in this space = overwhelmed and lost (deservedly so).
Phrases to use:
"Ignore the noise"
"Start simple"
"You're not behind"
"We'll build this correctly together"
Position yourself as a PARTNER, not a dollar sign relationship.
Always have a next step before next session:
Examples:
List all the tools you have
Map all data locations
Define three use cases
Get budget approval (could take multiple sessions)
Pick pilot department
Assign a champion
The 60-Minute Call Structure:
0-5 min: Pain and goal
5-15 min: Real discovery
15-25 min: Diagnosing
25-35 min: Recommendation (walk through why it might not be realistic for their business)
35-40 min: Next steps
Call checklist:
- Start with pain/goal
- Ask scale questions
- Map their stack (mentally if you think in workflows)
- Find knowledge gaps
- Give HONEST advice
- Warn of pitfalls
- Show alternatives (different ways to solve same thing, which are quicker/cheaper)
- Offer pricing tiers
"The more reps you get in, the more readily available this information will be for you."

lessons.title: 5) The Call "Autopsy" Protocol 📲 🔎
lessons.description:
You're probably not as good at discovery calls as you think you are 😳
You can use Gemini 2.5 Pro's video input capability to audit your own performance, catch verbal and non-verbal mistakes you don't notice, and systematically improve every call you take.
What you'll watch:
The "Arya" prompt system that reviews your calls frame-by-frame
Scorecard framework: Clarity, vocal delivery, body language, questioning, client engagement
Real autopsy of an actual client call (name redacted)
How to catch filler words, pacing issues, and moments where clients disengage
Why AI feedback hits different than human feedbackThe brutal reality:
"You can get curveballs left and right. Sometimes it takes 30-40 minutes for someone to get to the point of why you're there to begin with. You assume it's either a good call or bad call, rarely neutral."
Most consultants take the outcome at face value. Winners dissect every call systematically.
The problem with self-assessment:
On the call:
- You think you're articulate
- You think you're smiley and composed
- You think your points are landing
Reality:
- You used 47 filler words in 15 minutes
- Client's body language showed confusion at 7:35
- You leaned back the entire call (signals low engagement)
- You spoke for 45 minutes of a 60-minute "discovery" call
You need an external audit. Human feedback = defensive reactions. AI feedback = neutral truth you can actually absorb.

---
The Arya System (Full Prompt Framework):
Persona setup:
"You are Arya, an expert in communication and executive presence coaching specializing in high-stakes B2B technology consulting. Your methodology combines principles of linguistic analysis, sales psychology, and nonverbal communication."
Task:
"Analyze the attached video. I need a comprehensive, brutally honest, yet productively constructive performance review. Your feedback should be direct, but framed as opportunities for improvement, focusing on actionable advice."
The scorecard categories:
1. Clarity (How clear were you?)
2. Vocal Delivery
3. Authority
4. Body Language and Presence
5. Questioning and Listening Skills
6. Client Engagement and Resonance (Did your points land?)
"These things you can see in person easily. Posture. Tone. But virtually, much harder to gauge on the fly."
How to use it:
1. Record call on Fireflies, Zoom, Google Meet, or Fathom
2. Download the video file (doesn't need high resolution)
3. Upload to Gemini (accepts video input)
4. Run the Arya prompt
5. Get timestamps, quotes, and specific moments to improve
Critical: Only do this if calls don't have sensitive client information.
Breakdown by principle requested:
Principle 1 - Clear Articulation:
- Are you structured and concise?
- Filler words and pauses (uhh, uh, you know)
Principle 2 - Verbal and Nonverbal Cues:
- Eye contact (or looking up when ideating)
- Posture and confidence
- Gestures (are you moving hands too much?)
Real comment from YouTube: "Someone told me to tie my hands together. Interesting. I actually more consciously see what I'm doing with my hands now."
Principle 3 - Client Analysis:
- Analyze CLIENT's body language throughout call
- Pinpoint moments they seem convinced, unsure, or skeptical
- Timestamps with quotes: "This is where you could have done better"
Principle 4 - Ask More, Say Less:
- Talk-to-listen ratio
- Are you giving them space to process?
Principle 5 - Storytelling and Analogies:
- Did you articulate thoughts in a consumable way?
- Did analogies land?
Output request:
"List top three most impactful things I can focus on to improve my next client call."

---
Real autopsy example (actual call breakdown):
Executive Summary:
"High energy session where your passion and deep subject matter expertise were clearly evident. This strength is currently coupled with a rapid-fire delivery that risks overwhelming the client and undermines your authority."
Scorecard results:
- Client Engagement: Amazing
- Questioning and Listening Skills: Clearly not the best
- (Other categories scored and broken down)
Actionable feedback received:
Issue 1 - Over-indexing on ideas:
"Your mind moves exceptionally fast. But you tend to present a fire hose of ideas without sufficient breaks for the client to process. At [timestamp], you rapidly list at least five distinct complex concepts in 12 seconds. This barrage can cause a senior client to disengage from the details and simply wait for the storm to pass."
Fix: Rule of Three
"When brainstorming, limit yourself to the top three points."
Issue 2 - Filler words:
Primary fillers: "like," "you know," "right" (with upward inflection)
"These are the most prevalent." [Shows exact timestamps where they occurred]
Real reaction: "I usually don't have these. I pride myself on speaking decently well presenting-wise. But in a call, you're taken from your zone of comfort into a different zone."
Issue 3 - Fear of silence:
"You often use a filler word to bridge the gap between your thoughts."
Nuance discovered: "I've used pauses before. Then clients will use it to speak over me."
Context matters for feedback interpretation.
Body language breakdown received:
Eye Contact:
"Strong and consistent. Minor natural breaks when thinking at 7:35 are acceptable."
Posture:
"You're leaned back for much of the call. While this can signal relaxation, for high-stakes C-suite conversation, slightly leaning forward non-verbally communicates higher engagement."
Context revealed: "This was me in a hotel in Dominican Republic working from there. I can totally see how I would be more relaxed than normal."
Gestures:
"Your energy is fantastic." (More praise than critique here)
Client body language analysis:
Moments of Conviction:
"Client was most engaged when you provided clear, actionable frameworks. He nods his head affirmatively and leans in slightly when you start to discuss concrete models like RICE."
Moments of Uncertainty:
"Client displayed contemplative or slightly overwhelmed body language when your pace accelerated." [Exact timestamps provided]

---
Speech mastery feedback:
Pacing issue:
"Many of your declarative statements end with an upward inflection. Like: 'And that's a huge opportunity, right?'"
Why this happens: "Sometimes I do that to make sure the person on the other end of the line is still with me."
AI catches the pattern you rationalize away.
Talk-to-listen ratio:
"Ratio is heavily skewed towards you talking."
Context provided: "This client wanted to listen more than they wanted to share with me."
Lesson: "Pull out some nuance. Keep in mind all your cases will be different."
Why AI feedback works better than human feedback:
"If anyone ever told me this themselves, I would definitely go into defensive mode. But because AI is neutral, I will take it more without the grain of salt."
Human feedback = ego protection kicks in
AI feedback = pure data you can act on
The systematic improvement loop:
Record every call (with permission)
Run Arya analysis within 24 hours
Note top 3 improvements
Practice those 3 things on next call
Re-analyze next call
6Track improvement over timeSpeaking headlines principle:
Instead of: Five complex concepts in 12 seconds
Do: Three clear points with pauses betweenInstead of: 45 minutes of you talking
Do: 20 minutes talking, 25 minutes listening, 15 minutes co-creatingInstead of: Leaning back entire call
Do: Lean slightly forward during key momentsThe compounding effect:
Week 1: Identify you use "like" 47 times per call
Week 2: Down to 23 times
Week 4: Down to 5 times
Week 8: Clients describe you as "articulate and confident"
Small fixes compound into massive presence upgrades.Critical reminder:
"A lot of times you will get a client that pushes your boundaries of how well composed you can be. Other times, it's on you. You've had an off day, busy day, might not have given 100% to someone that paid for your time."
The Arya system catches both: When it's the client being difficult, and when you're off your game.
The full prompt will be attached to this post. Upload to Gemini. Get your autopsy. Improve systematically.
Next episode: Handling difficult clients and navigating political landmines in enterprise deals.

lessons.title: 7) Why Communication Is EVERYTHING 🗣️
lessons.description:
Communication beats coding & n8n ability. Every. Single. Time.
This video is way longer than usual, but I'm very passionate about this topic, because few things matter more
~40 minutes on the business communication rubric that determines whether clients hire you, trust you, and refer you—regardless of how well you know N8N or Claude Code.
What you'll watch:
The university-level communication scoring system (verbal + non-verbal breakdown)
Pre-call AI research workflow (Perplexity → N8N workflow generation in 15 minutes)
Discovery framework: Problem scoping, requirements gathering, constraints
The "ask why 5 times" technique for getting to root problems
How to handle accents and improve articulation (speech coach hack)The brutal truth: It doesn't matter how smart you are at coding, vibe coding, Make.com, N8N. If you suck at communicating, if you don't have proper verbiage, proper way to frame problems, show you're listening—it doesn't matter how good you are. You won't get clients. Or if you get clients, you won't retain them.Communication is everything.
The background story:
This comes from teaching Business Communication Skills for 5 years at university.
Personal journey: Failed first presentation (got 51%). Eventually did so well they asked him to teach the course. Used to do competitive French and Spanish debates. Started as introverted, shy, pure nerd.
"My operating system is as dry as a rock. I've had to put makeup and teach myself to be a real human being over time instead of a bot that just does Claude Code."
The university rubric (adapted for consulting):
Original rubric: 5-minute presentation with PowerPoint, scored on:
Setup/Agenda
Body content
Conclusion
Transitions
Message clarity
Creativity
Verbal communication
Non-verbal communicationReal student example shown: 56 "ums" in 5-minute presentation.
"How many times do you think people got distracted or stopped paying attention? If you can't articulate a thought succinctly and concisely, it doesn't matter how great the solution is. People won't trust you."
Verbal Communication Breakdown:
Voice control:
- Speed
- Intonation (critical for authority)
- Projection
Clarity and fluency:
- Filler words (uh, um, like, you know)
- Every filler word = listener distraction
- Can't demonstrate mastery with constant fillers
The upward inflection problem:
Bad example: "Are you looking for some form of automation service?"
This sounds like you're asking permission, being subservient, at the beck and call of customer.
Good example: Downward inflection on declarative statements. Confident, not questioning.
"Many declarative statements end with upward inflection. Like: 'And that's a huge opportunity, right?' This undermines authority."
Non-Verbal Communication Breakdown:
Projected confidence and mastery:
Shadowed people on first sales calls: "Complete fear in their voice"
Everything was upward intonation
Made them sound unconfidentFacial expression:
Especially important on Zoom
Technical folks often don't care about being animated
Explaining with passion matters"Non-technical people have advantage here. But if you're technical AND can do verbals/non-verbals, you become hard to beat on the battlefield."
Eye contact (critical on video calls):
"I visually look at the camera lens itself. I don't look at the screen. When delivering a message, I want to look piercingly through this camera to get to the other person."
Why it matters: Strong eye contact shows you're not lying. People who lie look to the side. Exaggerators look to the left.

lessons.title: 8) The Chinese Menu Technique 🥡 🥢
lessons.description:
A client asked for our "Chinese menu" on a discovery call...
We had no idea what they meant.
Now it's how we're going to approach closing even more education deals (and maybe you should too)
9 minutes on packaging your consulting services the way Fortune 500 companies expect to see them -and why this format makes clients say "we want 3, 4, 6, and the light version of 8."
What you'll watch:
Why companies call this a "Chinese menu" (and how to build yours)
The tier structure: Appetizers → Soups → Intermediate → Advanced → Desserts → Banquets
Using Claude to auto-format professional Docx menus (ChatGPT can't do this yet)
Real example: AI Workshop Menu 2025 with 30+ offerings
How to use this for both education and technical consultingThe origin story:
Three discovery calls deep with a financial sector client. They asked: "Can you send us your Chinese menu?"
Response: "...deer in headlights. Had no idea what they were referring to."
Their explanation: "In a Chinese menu, you have tens or hundreds of items across 5-6 pages. Give us enough variety of what you could teach our team so they can pick specific items."
Built them a literal Chinese menu (not well formatted initially). Listed as Order #1, Order #2, Order #3, etc.
Closing call: "We want 3, 4, 6, and the light version of 8."
That's when it clicked. This is genius for packaging consulting services, especially education-heavy engagements.
Why this works:
Most consultants: Send vague proposal with 2-3 generic service tiers
You: Send menu with 30+ specific, categorized offerings
Result: Clients can mix and match exactly what they need. No full-length conversation needed—just pick from the menu.
The structure (5 tiers + bundles):
Appetizers (Beginner Level):
- ChatGPT Mastery (Zero to Hero)
- Claude Mastery
- Gemini Essentials
- Prompt Engineering 101
- Custom GPTs and Claude Projects
- AI for Daily Productivity
- Voice AI and Conversational Interfaces
- AI Search and Research
- Reasoning Models Deep Dive
- Memory and Personalization in AI
Why ChatGPT/Claude basics? "One of the best ways to get foot in door of all kinds of companies—SMBs to enterprises. They want teams to use ChatGPT the RIGHT way to fullest potential."
Custom GPTs = crowd-pleasers. Always include.
Soups (Practical Wins):
Document Intelligence and Analysis
AI Meeting Assistance and Transcription
AI-Powered Research Workflows
Data Analysis with AI
AI for Presentations and Storytelling (Gamma, Beautiful AI)
Building Prompt Libraries
AI for Social Media ContentThese are quick wins that show immediate value.Intermediate Level:
How Transformers Work (nuts and bolts of LLMs)
Image Generation Mastery
Video Generation Tools
Multimodal AI Applications
RAG Implementation (big crowd-pleaser)
MCP Server Development
Agentic Workflows
-Coding Basics for Non-Developers (0 to 30%, not 80%)Note: "How Transformers Work is not common request. But it has happened. Some companies appreciate the nuts and bolts."Advanced Level:
AI Coding Tools (Cursor, Windsurf, Replit)
Claude Code and Computer Use
Building Production AI Agents
API Integration Without Coding
Building AI-Powered Apps
Voice Agent Development
Custom Automation PlatformsThis is where you can offer "light versions"—like showing tools without teaching coding behind them.Desserts (C-suite Oriented):
AI for Business Strategy
AI for Investment and Due Diligence
AI for HR and Talent Management
AI for Marketing Transformation
AI for Sales Enablement
AI for Finance and OperationsWhy separate C-suite tier? "Core employees want meat and potatoes. C-suite wants 100,000-foot view. Even telling them there's N8N and Make.com is reasonable amount of information."
C-suite questions: Which tool lets employees go faster? Which is cheaper at scale? Which has better security? Where can we get a deal?
Banquet Options (Pre-Packaged Bundles):
Instead of clients picking 15 individual items, offer pre-curated packages:
Banquet A: Foundation Package
Banquet B: Technical Implementation Package
Banquet C: Leadership Strategy Package
Banquet D: Full Transformation Package
Banquet E: Custom Tailored (they pick)
What's included with banquets:
Template library
Custom GPT setup guides
Workflow automation templates
30-day post-workshop email support ✨The upsell opportunity: "This could be your entry point to offer small retainer or big retainer, depending on who you're dealing with."The formatting hack (Claude only):
ChatGPT can't do this level of Docx formatting yet. Claude can.
How to use it:
Enable Claude's code execution and file creation in Settings → Capabilities
Upload the template Docx (attached to this post)
Ask Claude to customize for your offerings
It creates high-fidelity formatted documentsReal prompt used: "Do deep research on latest and greatest topics in AI. Supplement with my old workshop lectures. Create Chinese menu format."
Result: Professional AI Workshop Menu 2025 (attached)Each item includes:
Module name
Duration (90-150 minutes delivery time, NOT prep time)
Difficulty tier
Brief descriptionThe delivery details section:
Mix and Match: Choose any combination to create your perfect workshop
Duration: 2-2.5 hours per session
Format: Remote or on-site (specify both options)
Updated: October 2025 (update monthly as tools change)
Footer message: "Serving fresh AI knowledge updated for October 2025. Things will change, tools will change, models will change."
This signals you stay current and clients need ongoing support.How to customize for your niche:
Take this structure, adapt categories:
For automation consulting:
Appetizers: Basic n8n/Make workflows
Soups: Quick automation wins**PIN: https://www.skool.com/earlyaidopters/consulting-playbook-day-8-the-chinese-menu-technique?p=767d5294

Response: "...deer in headlights. Had no idea what they were referring to."
Their explanation: "In a Chinese menu, you have tens or hundreds of items across 5-6 pages. Give us enough variety of what you could teach our team so they can pick specific items."
Built them a literal Chinese menu (not well formatted initially). Listed as Order #1, Order #2, Order #3, etc.
Closing call: "We want 3, 4, 6, and the light version of 8."
That's when it clicked. This is genius for packaging consulting services, especially education-heavy engagements.
Why this works:
Most consultants: Send vague proposal with 2-3 generic service tiers
You: Send menu with 30+ specific, categorized offerings
Result: Clients can mix and match exactly what they need. No full-length conversation needed—just pick from the menu.
The structure (5 tiers + bundles):
Appetizers (Beginner Level):
- ChatGPT Mastery (Zero to Hero)
- Claude Mastery
- Gemini Essentials
- Prompt Engineering 101
- Custom GPTs and Claude Projects
- AI for Daily Productivity
- Voice AI and Conversational Interfaces
- AI Search and Research
- Reasoning Models Deep Dive
- Memory and Personalization in AI
Why ChatGPT/Claude basics? "One of the best ways to get foot in door of all kinds of companies—SMBs to enterprises. They want teams to use ChatGPT the RIGHT way to fullest potential."
Custom GPTs = crowd-pleasers. Always include.
Soups (Practical Wins):
Document Intelligence and Analysis
AI Meeting Assistance and Transcription
AI-Powered Research Workflows
Data Analysis with AI
AI for Presentations and Storytelling (Gamma, Beautiful AI)
Building Prompt Libraries
AI for Social Media Content
These are quick wins that show immediate value.
Intermediate Level:
How Transformers Work (nuts and bolts of LLMs)
Image Generation Mastery
Video Generation Tools
Multimodal AI Applications
RAG Implementation (big crowd-pleaser)
MCP Server Development
Agentic Workflows
-Coding Basics for Non-Developers (0 to 30%, not 80%)
Note: "How Transformers Work is not common request. But it has happened. Some companies appreciate the nuts and bolts."
Advanced Level:
AI Coding Tools (Cursor, Windsurf, Replit)
Claude Code and Computer Use
Building Production AI Agents
API Integration Without Coding
Building AI-Powered Apps
Voice Agent Development
Custom Automation Platforms
This is where you can offer "light versions"—like showing tools without teaching coding behind them.
Desserts (C-suite Oriented):
AI for Business Strategy
AI for Investment and Due Diligence
AI for HR and Talent Management
AI for Marketing Transformation
AI for Sales Enablement
AI for Finance and Operations
Why separate C-suite tier? "Core employees want meat and potatoes. C-suite wants 100,000-foot view. Even telling them there's N8N and
Make.com
is reasonable amount of information."
C-suite questions: Which tool lets employees go faster? Which is cheaper at scale? Which has better security? Where can we get a deal?
Banquet Options (Pre-Packaged Bundles):
Instead of clients picking 15 individual items, offer pre-curated packages:
Banquet A: Foundation Package
Banquet B: Technical Implementation Package
Banquet C: Leadership Strategy Package
Banquet D: Full Transformation Package
Banquet E: Custom Tailored (they pick)
What's included with banquets:
Template library
Custom GPT setup guides
Workflow automation templates
30-day post-workshop email support ✨
The upsell opportunity: "This could be your entry point to offer small retainer or big retainer, depending on who you're dealing with."
The formatting hack (Claude only):
ChatGPT can't do this level of Docx formatting yet. Claude can.
How to use it:
Enable Claude's code execution and file creation in Settings → Capabilities
Upload the template Docx (attached to this post)
Ask Claude to customize for your offerings
It creates high-fidelity formatted documents
Real prompt used: "Do deep research on latest and greatest topics in AI. Supplement with my old workshop lectures. Create Chinese menu format."

Each item includes:
Module name
Duration (90-150 minutes delivery time, NOT prep time)
Difficulty tier
Brief description
The delivery details section:
Mix and Match: Choose any combination to create your perfect workshop
Duration: 2-2.5 hours per session
Format: Remote or on-site (specify both options)
Updated: October 2025 (update monthly as tools change)
Footer message: "Serving fresh AI knowledge updated for October 2025. Things will change, tools will change, models will change."
This signals you stay current and clients need ongoing support.
How to customize for your niche:
Take this structure, adapt categories:
For automation consulting:
Appetizers: Basic n8n/Make workflows
Soups: Quick automation wins

lessons.title: 9) Learning from Failure
lessons.description:
A Consultant's Reflection 💡
Today I walk you through a rare but recent failure of mine.
We're dissecting a $300 refund and the Golden Parrot Strategy that would've prevented it 🦜
13 minutes on why correct advice delivered lazily loses clients, how to package borrowed expertise as white-glove service, and the 3 red flags that should've made me reject this consult.
What you'll watch:
Real refund breakdown: PPC ads consulting gone wrong
The "Golden Parrot Strategy" for repackaging existing solutions
Red flags that scream "reject this client"
How to over-deliver when you're not the domain expert
Why clients care more about packaging than correctnessThe brutal stats:
Only refunded 2 consults since starting Prompt Advisers in 2022.
Most recent one: Few weeks ago.
Instead of hiding it: Full autopsy of what went wrong.
The setup:
Client came through Fiverr (rare, supposed to be blocked but they'd consulted before so permissions allowed it).
Their requirements:
Upskill PPC team on Google Ads, Meta Ads, TikTok Ads with AI
Generate super advertisement concepts for clients
"Use AI, practical usage, not just show us ten tools and good luck" ⚠️
After consultation, show team how to use AI for e-commerce ads, product ads, UGC ads, lead ads, building media assetsContext: English not their first language. European client. High expectations from someone with zero background in those areas.
🚩 Red flag #1 that should've made me reject:
"Practical usage, not just show us ten tools and good luck."
This was the clue. Don't be lazy in delivery. But I missed it.🚩 Red flag #2 that should've made me reject:
"I don't have a background in pay-per-click. I know how it works. I've done a project involving it. But I'm not an industry expert."
I'm good at AI. I'm good at solutioning tools and neural pathways. But this person wanted specific, critical path solution. Not general conceptualization.🚩 Red flag #3 that should've made me reject:
The scope was massive for 30 minutes. Building media assets, UGC ads, product ads, lead ads—all specialized domains I haven't run campaigns in.
"I know how to build UGC using Sora and Veo. Technically, I got it on lock. But I assumed I could just give instructions and they'd be happy."Wrong assumption.
What actually happened on the call:
Gave honest disclaimer: "I'm not a PPC expert. You probably realized that from our first consult (which was SEO-focused)."
Gave rational advice: "There's this person, Robon August. Decent-sized YouTube channel, big community. He specializes in UGC.**PIN: https://www.skool.com/earlyaidopters/consulting-playbook-day-9-learn-from-my-recent-consulting-failure?p=74abd343
