lessons.title: 19) How to Run a Calm, Effective Sales Call
lessons.description: The speaker explains that a successful sales call is less about pitching and more about listening, understanding, and guiding the conversation naturally. Instead of scripted selling or forced small talk, the focus should be on asking good questions, matching the prospect’s level of knowledge, and positioning yourself as a helpful consultant rather than a salesperson. By discussing outcomes in plain language, showing the product in action, and involving the prospect in shaping the solution, trust is built without pressure. Because the initial offer is low risk, the seller can stay relaxed and detached from the outcome, which actually increases confidence and credibility. The overall goal is to build a relationship, deliver value early, and create space for long term collaboration rather than forcing a single sale.

lessons.title: 20) Building Your First AI Agent Step by Step
lessons.description: The speaker walks through the practical process of building an AI chatbot using n8n, OpenAI, and a simple chat widget, showing how all the pieces connect from backend to frontend. They explain how to import a ready made workflow, connect it to an OpenAI model with an API key, and configure the agent’s behavior using a clear prompting framework that defines context, actions, rules, output style, and safety. The agent is trained by uploading business data like scraped website content, allowing it to answer questions, capture leads, and route customer service requests appropriately. The workflow is designed to be duplicated easily for new clients by swapping prompts, data, and notification details. Finally, the chatbot is deployed through a front end widget that can be embedded on any website, demonstrating how quickly a functional, client ready AI agent can be built and customized.

lessons.title: How to Sell AI Solutions Masterclass
lessons.description:
Presented by Cleve - 20+ Years Sales Experience
---
The CALM Framework
- Curious - Lead with questions, not pitches. Understand the client's real issue
- Authentic - Drop the robotic scripts. Be yourself
- Listening - Sales is not manipulative when you're genuinely helping. View sales as service
- Close with ease - Focus on where you lose sales (discovery), not just the close
---
Discovery Calls: Where 80% of Sales Happen
Key insight: If you're doing all the talking, you're guessing what they need. If they're talking, they're telling you what they need.
Surface Questions vs. Root Questions
Surface (Low Value):
- Budget questions
- Basic rapport
- General pain points
Root (High Value):
- "What's the cost of inaction today?"
- "Who else is impacted by this bottleneck?"
- "Why now? Why is this urgent?"
Hidden Pain Points
- Clients often don't know their actual problem (they see smoke, not the fire)
- Some play cards close to their chest (been burned before, or already have a competitor in mind)
- Ask: "What are you really trying to achieve?" and "What's it actually costing you?"
---
Funnel Stages & How to Identify Them
Top of Funnel (Problem Aware)
- Questions to ask: "What made you reach out now?" / "What happens if you don't solve this in 6 months?"
- Your role: Teacher - validate pain, educate on root causes
Middle of Funnel (Solution Seeking)
- Questions to ask: "Why do you think Method X is the right fit?" / "What metrics would you like to see change?"
- Your role: Strategic Advisor - differentiate yourself, sell the transformation
Bottom of Funnel (Decision Ready)
- Questions to ask: "What happens if we delay the start by 30 days?"
- Your role: Implementation Partner - handle logistics, make it easy
---
Reading the Room: 5 Energy Signals
1. Voice - Getting quieter? Getting excited? The "lean in"?
2. Language Patterns
- "I should..." = External, non-committal
- "I need to..." = Motivated
- "I'll try..." = Possibly could
- "I will..." = Commitment
3. Story vs. Solution Mode - Are they sharing emotion or just logistics?
4. Resistance Patterns - "What if...", "I've tried...", "That's great, but..."
5. Enrollment Language - "If I do this...", "When I get access..." = STOP TALKING, they've sold themselves
---
Three Cognitive Biases That Drive Buying
1. Loss Aversion - Pain of losing > pleasure of gaining
- Reframe: "Every week you wait is another $5K client slipping through"
2. Social Proof - They want to know others have done it
- Reframe: "This is the same roadblock my client hit last month..."
3. Sunk Cost - How much more will they waste trying alone?
- Reframe: "You've already invested X hours figuring this out..."
---
The Three-Step Closing Sequence
1. Recap the solution - Mirror back what you heard using their words
2. Tie to their goals - "This will help you achieve X"
3. Assumptive close - "When would you like to get started? I have Tuesday or Thursday next week"
Never ask: "What do you think? Should we pursue this?" - You just handed them all the power back.
---
Critical Rules
- Always Book a Meeting from a Meeting (BAMFAM) - Give 2 specific options, not "when works for you?"
- "Let me think about it" with no next step = You're getting ghosted
- Clients who negotiate hard on price = Your worst clients - Those who sign without haggling become your best advocates
- Build rapport in 2-3 minutes max - Then move to substance
- Mirror their energy - High energy person? Match it. Internal processor? Slow down
---
Biggest Mistakes People Make
1. Talking too much instead of listening
2. Selling features instead of transformation
3. Leaving calls without defined next steps
4. Giving pricing before establishing value
5. Chasing every lead instead of qualifying
---
When Asked for Price Too Early
Response: "I could tell you a million dollars right now, but I need to understand what's happening so I can give you an accurate price. Some clients spend $40, some spend $40,000 - it depends on what you need."
---
Platform Strategy by Funnel Stage
- YouTube - Middle + Bottom (trust building, tutorials)
- LinkedIn - Middle + Bottom (thought leadership)
- Email (your list) - Middle + Bottom (nurturing)
- TikTok/Instagram - Top of Funnel only

lessons.title: How to Get Them to Show Up on the Call
Your Week 1 Homework
lessons.description:
You've now got the foundations down: the C³ framework (Capture → Convince → Convert) and how every paid acquisition funnel actually works.
This week's job is to do the groundwork so that next week, when we go deeper and start optimizing your landing page, you already have something real to optimize. Don't skip this, the people who do the homework are the ones who'll get the most out of next week.
There are three tasks. Do them in order.
Task 1 — Create Your Offer
Before you write a single ad or build a single page, you need to know exactly what you're selling and why anyone should care.
Write out your offer in one or two sentences. Be specific. "I help businesses with AI" is not an offer. "I build AI chatbots that handle customer support for e-commerce stores so they cut response time by 80%" is an offer.
Answer these:
- What exactly are you selling? (the automation, the audit, the chatbot, the buildout)
- Who is it for? (the specific type of business / person)
- What's the outcome? (what changes for them after they buy)
- Why you? (what makes it believable coming from you)
Don't overthink it. Get a v1 down. We'll sharpen it as we go.
Task 2 — Do Your Market Research
This is the part most people skip — and it's the part that makes everything else easier. You're not guessing what your customer wants. You're going to find out, in their own words.
Pull out and write down all the important stuff about your ideal customer:
- Who they are — their role, their business, their situation
- The problem they're dealing with that your offer solves
- What they've already tried that didn't work
- What they're afraid of (e.g. being left behind in the AI space, wasting money, looking stupid)
- What they actually want — the real outcome, the dream scenario
- The exact words and phrases they use to describe their problem
Where to find this: their social posts, Reddit threads, YouTube comments, reviews of competitors, forum discussions, sales call notes — anywhere your ideal customer talks about their problem. Steal their language. The words they use are the words that should end up on your page.
Save all of this. You'll feed it into Task 3.
Task 3 — Build Your Landing Page Mockup (with AI)
Now you take everything from Tasks 1 and 2 and turn it into a first-draft landing page using the AI prompt below.
This is just a mockup, a starting point. It will not be perfect, and that's the point. Next week we're going to go deep on optimizing this, so all you need right now is a v1 that exists.

Write out your offer in one or two sentences. Be specific. "I help businesses with AI" is not an offer. "I build AI chatbots that handle customer support for e-commerce stores so they cut response time by 80%" is an offer.
Answer these:
What exactly are you selling?
(the automation, the audit, the chatbot, the buildout)
Who is it for?
(the specific type of business / person)
What's the outcome?
(what changes for them after they buy)
Why you?
(what makes it believable coming from you)
Don't overthink it. Get a v1 down. We'll sharpen it as we go.
Task 2 — Do Your Market Research
This is the part most people skip — and it's the part that makes everything else easier. You're not guessing what your customer wants. You're going to find out, in their own words.
Pull out and write down all the important stuff about your
ideal customer
Who they are
— their role, their business, their situation
The problem
they're dealing with that your offer solves
What they've already tried
that didn't work
What they're afraid of
(e.g. being left behind in the AI space, wasting money, looking stupid)
What they actually want
— the real outcome, the dream scenario
The exact words and phrases they use
to describe their problem
Where to find this: their social posts, Reddit threads, YouTube comments, reviews of competitors, forum discussions, sales call notes — anywhere your ideal customer talks about their problem.
Steal their language.
The words they use are the words that should end up on your page.
Save all of this. You'll feed it into Task 3.
Task 3 — Build Your Landing Page Mockup (with AI)
Now you take everything from Tasks 1 and 2 and turn it into a first-draft landing page using the AI prompt below.
This is just a
mockup
, a starting point. It will not be perfect, and that's the point.
Next week we're going to go deep on optimizing this
, so all you need right now is a v1 that exists.

lessons.title: iii) The Mental Model That Changes Everything
lessons.description:
Lesson 1: The Mental Model That Changes Everything
Claude Code isn't a chatbot. It's the same brain with different hands. Get this wrong and nothing else in the course clicks.
What you'll learn:
- The "Ferrari vs bicycle" framing for understanding AI-assisted development
- How the agentic loop works under the hood
- The seven core tools Claude Code uses (Read, Write, Edit, Glob, Grep, Bash, Agent)
- When to use Plan mode to think before acting
- How worktrees and scheduling let you run multiple sessions in parallel
- Why this mental model is the foundation every other lesson builds on
Key takeaway:
"Same brain, different hands. Claude Code doesn't think differently than Claude. It just has access to your filesystem, your terminal, and your git history."
Best for: Developers and non-developers alike who want the foundational mental model before touching the terminal.

lessons.title: iv) What Claude Code Actually Does
lessons.description:
Lesson 2: What Claude Code Actually Does
Most people use Claude Code without understanding how it thinks. This lesson cracks open the agentic loop so you can work with it, not against it.
What you'll learn:
- The four-step agentic loop: observe, plan, execute, check
- Why the "contractor" analogy is the most useful way to think about Claude Code
- How Claude Code maintains state awareness across a conversation
- The self-correction mechanism that catches and fixes its own mistakes
- Why treating it like a junior developer sets the right expectations
- Common mistakes people make when they misunderstand the loop
Key takeaway:
"A contractor doesn't read your mind. They read the blueprint. Your job is to hand them a good one."
Best for: Anyone who has used Claude Code but felt like they were guessing at how it works.

lessons.title: vi) GUI vs CLI (Why the Terminal Matters)
lessons.description:
Lesson 4: GUI vs CLI (Why the Terminal Matters)
If you've avoided the terminal your whole life, this lesson is your on-ramp. If you already live in it, you'll learn why Claude Code makes it even more powerful.
What you'll learn:
- Why transparency in the CLI beats the black box of a GUI
- The DSP shortcut that saves time every single session
- Essential terminal commands: cd, pwd, ls
- A terminal starter kit you can use starting on day one
- How Claude Code itself becomes your terminal translator when you get stuck
- The mindset shift from "I need to learn commands" to "I need to describe what I want"
Key takeaway:
"You don't need to master the terminal. You need to be comfortable enough to let Claude Code do the heavy lifting inside it."
Best for: Non-developers, designers, and operators who want to stop being afraid of the command line.

lessons.title: vii) Full Stack (API, CLI, MCP, Skills)
lessons.description:
Lesson 5: The Full Stack (API, CLI, MCP, Skills)
There are four layers to the Claude ecosystem. Most people only use one. This lesson maps all four and shows you when each one is the right tool.
What you'll learn:
- The four layers: API, CLI, MCP, and Skills, and how they relate to each other
- When to drop down to the API vs staying in the CLI
- Real examples using AWS CLI, Google Workspace CLI, and Supabase CLI
- The decision matrix for choosing the right layer for any given task
- How MCP servers extend Claude Code's reach into external services
- Why skills sit on top of everything and when to build one instead of scripting
Key takeaway:
"The CLI is the starting point, not the ceiling. Knowing when to go deeper is what separates a user from a builder."
Best for: Intermediate users ready to understand the full ecosystem and stop leaving capabilities on the table.

lessons.title: viii) From API to CLI in Five Minutes
lessons.description:
From API to CLI in Five Minutes
Any API with documentation can become a command-line tool. This lesson proves it by building a full Calendly CLI in a single prompt.
What you'll learn:
- How Claude Code reads API docs and designs a CLI interface automatically
- The one-prompt workflow: paste the docs, describe the commands, let Claude build it
- A live demo building a working Calendly CLI from scratch
- Why this pattern works for virtually any REST API
- How to go from "I wish I had a CLI for this" to "I do" in under five minutes
Key takeaway:
"You don't need to wait for someone to build a CLI for your favorite service. Claude Code will read the docs and build one for you."
Best for: Developers and power users who interact with APIs regularly and want faster, terminal-native access to any service.

lessons.title: i) Context Engineering (The Concepts)
lessons.description:
Lesson 6: Context Engineering (The Concepts)
Context is the single biggest lever you have over Claude Code's output quality. This lesson teaches you how to engineer it like a professional.
What you'll learn:
- The contractor briefing analogy for understanding context
- Five tiers of context and how they stack together
- How to manage your token budget so Claude Code doesn't lose the plot mid-conversation
- Why your root CLAUDE.md should be 16 lines, not 160
- Skills as self-contained context capsules that load only when needed
- The three layers of persistent context: CLAUDE.md, rules, and skills
Key takeaway:
"Every token you waste on context that doesn't matter is a token stolen from context that does."
Best for: Anyone whose Claude Code sessions start strong but degrade halfway through, or anyone getting inconsistent results.

lessons.title: ii) Context Engineering (Applied)
lessons.description:
Lesson 7: Context Engineering (Applied)
Theory is over. This lesson walks you through a real CLAUDE.md overhaul, trimming 311 lines down to 29 while making it more effective.
What you'll learn:
- How to use the /context command to audit what Claude Code is actually reading
- The root node diet: cutting bloat without losing signal
- Rules with glob patterns that activate only when relevant files are touched
- How to build a hierarchical CLAUDE.md structure across a project
- The garden metaphor: context is a living thing that needs pruning
Key takeaway:
"A bloated CLAUDE.md doesn't make Claude smarter. It makes Claude confused. Cut until it hurts, then cut a little more."
Best for: Anyone who has a CLAUDE.md file that's grown out of control, or anyone setting one up for the first time.

lessons.title: iii) Executing Context Isolation
lessons.description:
Lesson 8: Context Isolation
One conversation doing everything is a recipe for disaster. This lesson teaches you how to keep Claude Code sessions clean, focused, and reusable.
What you'll learn:
- Why you should run one terminal per domain, not one terminal for everything
- The difference between conversation mining and /resume, and when to use each
- How to name and organize sessions so you can find and reuse them later
- The continuous improvement flywheel: use, review, refine, repeat
- The garden metaphor applied to session maintenance and context hygiene
- Practical patterns for splitting work across isolated conversations
Key takeaway:
"The fastest way to ruin a Claude Code session is to let it accumulate context from three unrelated tasks."
Best for: Users who find their Claude Code sessions getting confused or producing lower quality output as conversations get longer.

lessons.title: iv) Executing Subagent Patterns
lessons.description:
Subagent Patterns
Four proven patterns for delegating work to subagents. Know when to investigate, when to execute, when to parallelize, and when to simplify.
What you'll learn:
- The code review pattern: let a subagent audit your code before you merge
- Explore then act: separate investigation from execution for safer, more confident changes
- Parallel tests: run multiple test suites simultaneously through subagents
- The simplifier pattern: hand off complex code for targeted refactoring
- Agent teams vs subagents and when each approach fits your situation
- How to structure prompts that delegate clearly without losing control
Key takeaway:
"The power move isn't doing everything yourself. It's knowing which tasks to hand off, and to which type of agent."
Best for: Users comfortable with Claude Code who want to scale their output by running multiple agents on different parts of a problem.

lessons.title: v) Dealing with Large Codebases
lessons.description:
Lesson 12: Large Codebases
Claude Code works great on small projects. But what happens when you point it at 12,000 lines of code? This lesson shows you how to scope, navigate, and conquer large repos.
What you'll learn:
- The scoping problem: why Claude Code struggles with big codebases by default
- The FleetOps demo: navigating a 12K-line codebase live
- How hierarchical CLAUDE.md files act as a navigation system for Claude Code
- The exploration playbook: understand first, investigate second, build last
- Prompt patterns that keep Claude Code focused instead of wandering across files
- How to structure your first message so Claude Code scopes correctly from the start
Key takeaway:
"In a large codebase, the prompt isn't the hard part. Scoping is. Tell Claude Code where to look before you tell it what to do."
Best for: Developers working on real production codebases who need Claude Code to stay focused and not wander.

lessons.description:
Lesson 9: Frameworks vs Vanilla
Everyone wants the magic framework. This lesson explains why most of them cost you more tokens than they save, and what to do instead.
What you'll learn:
- The framework trap cycle and why people keep falling into it
- Boris Cherny's real-world setup: 100 PRs per week with a 100-line CLAUDE.md
- The hidden token tax of frameworks like GSD2 and why it matters
- The "mine don't marry" principle for adopting external patterns
- The extraction playbook for pulling useful ideas out of any framework
- How to evaluate whether a framework is helping or hurting your output
Key takeaway:
"The best framework is the one you built yourself, one rule at a time, from patterns that actually worked in your codebase."
Best for: Anyone tempted to install a Claude Code framework, or anyone who already did and isn't sure it's helping.

i) The Meta Skill (Gemini Video)

Record yourself doing something once. Feed it to Gemini. Let Claude Code reverse-engineer the process. This is how you clone workflows, not just code.

Lesson 15: Skill Chaining
One command. Many skills. One result. This lesson shows you how to build conductor skills that chain multiple capabilities into automated workflows.
What you'll learn:
- How conductor skills use context:fork to orchestrate other skills
- The morning standup chain: /gmail, /convo-review, /google-calendar, /trend-pulse in one command
- How to collapse a 35-minute manual morning routine into 3 minutes
- The architecture of a conductor skill and how to build your own from scratch
- When chaining makes sense vs when you should keep skills separate
- How to debug a chain when one skill in the sequence fails
Key takeaway:
"A skill does one thing well. A conductor skill makes ten things work together. That's where the time savings get absurd."
Best for: Users who have built a few skills and are ready to combine them into automated daily workflows.

Rules are suggestions. Hooks are laws. This lesson introduces the mechanism that lets you enforce behavior automatically, with zero context cost.

- What hooks are and how they differ from rules and instructions
- The two main hook types: Stop hooks and PostToolUse hooks

"A rule says 'please don't do this.' A hook says 'you literally cannot do this.' That's the difference between a suggestion and a guardrail."
Best for: Anyone who wants automated safety checks, notifications, or enforced standards without burning context tokens.

- Your first hook: a step-by-step walkthrough you can follow along with

Best for:
Anyone who wants automated safety checks, notifications, or enforced standards without burning context tokens.

Eight battle-tested hooks you can install today. From credential protection to brand enforcement, each one solves a real problem with zero ongoing effort.

The AI Strategy Factory 🏭
lessons.description:
Imagine you could put the name of your/another company, a few details here and there, and get an entire set of files, roadmaps, and even a full report and powerpoint on what the 2026 AI strategy should be?
Well, imagine no more.
I spent around 4.5 hours putting this resource together, building on a decent number of tricks I've already showed you related to Claude Code and generating assets at scale.
🔗 GitHub Repo: https://github.com/promptadvisers/ai-strategy-factory
Clone it. Customize it. Use it to look like a legend.
What I built:
Two text boxes. Company name. Company description. Click submit. Get 15 markdown files, 2 PowerPoints, and 2 Word documents—a complete AI strategy deliverable suite generated automatically.
The deliverable list:
Markdown files (internal knowledge):
- Technology inventory and data infrastructure assessment
- Pain point matrix by department
- AI maturity model and readiness assessment
- 30/60/90/180/360-day implementation roadmap
- Quick wins list
- Vendor comparisons and build vs buy frameworks
- License consolidation recommendations
- ROI calculator and cost analysis framework
- Data governance and acceptable use policy template
- Prompt library starter kit
- Glossary of AI terms
- Department-specific use case library
- Change management and training playbook
PowerPoint files (polished delivery):
- AI strategy presentation deck
- Current state vs future state diagrams (rendered as actual images using Mermaid)
Word documents (formal reports):
- Final AI strategy report
- Statement of work template
The process I went through:
Phase 1 - Consulting Knowledge Synthesis
I downloaded playbooks from McKinsey, BCG, KPMG, OpenAI, and IBM—all the free guides these firms publish to show they know their stuff. Problem is, these PDFs are massive. 28 pages here, 46 pages there. Can't just dump them all into Claude Code without blowing the context window.
So I built a lazy agentic RAG system. Used Gemini 2.5 Flash (cheap, massive context window) to go through each PDF in 10,000 token chunks. For each chunk, I ran a synthesis prompt that extracted only the valuable nuggets—removing the buzzwords, the fluff, the repeated frameworks. End result: compressed cheat sheets of every consulting guide that I can feed into Claude Code without worrying about token limits.
Phase 2 - Skill Extraction
I needed Claude Code to know how to create DocX files, PowerPoints, Excel files, and PDFs. Instead of manually teaching it, I went straight to Anthropic's GitHub repo where they publish the exact Python functions Claude uses to generate these files. Pulled the skills directly from the source, had Claude learn from them, and documented the whole process in a skills reference file.
Phase 3 - Perplexity API Integration
Here's what makes this temporal and not cookie-cutter. I integrated the Perplexity API so that when you run this system, it does live research on the company. If you're running this in January 2026, it searches as of January 2026. If n8n gets replaced by something better, the system will know. If Claude Code gets superseded, the recommendations update.
I set it up with different research depths—quick mode for basic company intel, comprehensive mode for deep research. You choose at runtime so you control cost.
Phase 4 - The Factory Architecture
Built a phased implementation plan where Claude Code:
1. Takes your two inputs (company name + description)
2. Runs Perplexity research to understand the company, industry, competitors
3. Synthesizes findings with the consulting knowledge base
4. Generates all 19 deliverables in organized folders
5. Renders Mermaid diagrams as actual PNG images
6. Packages everything for download
Each phase checks off completion before moving to the next. If the context window maxes out (which happened to me twice during the build), you can spin up a new session and pick up where you left off using the to-do list it maintains.
Phase 5 - React Frontend
Simple interface. Company name field. Description text box. Research depth toggle. Submit button. All generated assets appear on screen with download links.
The technical reality:
This took multiple Claude Code sessions. I hit the context window limit. I had API errors. The Perplexity model name was wrong in the docs. Gemini chunking broke on one file. I'm showing you all of that in the long-form video because building in public means showing the mess, not just the result.
But here's the thing—all these assets are just words. They take fewer tokens than building a complex web app because you're not generating hundreds of lines of JavaScript and Python. You're asking AI to write organized documentation. Even on the $20 Claude plan, you can get away with a lot of this if you spread out your requests.
Why this matters:
Whether you're doing this for your own business, for yourself, or for someone else on a paid basis—this system lets you crank out strategy documentation that would take days to produce manually.
The whole point: minimum input, maximum professional output. You look like a legend. The client gets a comprehensive deliverable package. Everyone wins.

lessons.title: Document Polisher Claude Skill 📜
lessons.description:
I spent a couple hours creating a custom Claude Code skill that applies world-class brand styling to any document you generate
The Economist, McKinsey, Stripe
Pick a style, and it formats your docx accordingly.
Video attached to this post walking through the full build (about 20 minutes)
🔗 GitHub Repo: Claude Skills Document Polisher
→ Clone it
→ Swap the brands
→ Make it yours
What I built:
A skill that presents you with 10 brand options when invoked
Pick a number, and it applies that brand's colors, fonts, spacing, and heading structure to your document
The brand menu:
Editorial style: The Economist
Consulting style: McKinsey, Deloitte, KPMG
Tech style: Stripe, Apple, IBM
Design style: Notion, Linear, Figma
The process I went through:
Phase 1: Building the Firecrawl MCP Server 🔥
Remember the Firecrawl brand extract trick from a couple weeks ago?
I turned that into a proper MCP server so I could use it inside Claude Code whenever I want.
Used the /mcp slash command, fed it the API documentation for Firecrawl's branding endpoint, and it generated a working MCP server in one shot
Three tools: Extract Branding, Scrape with Branding, and Compare Branding.
Phase 2: Cloning and Augmenting the Skill 🧞‍♂️
Cloned Anthropic's skills repo into .claude (important: has to be inside .claude or Claude Code won't find it).
Told it to create a new skill called Document Polisher, based on the existing docx creator.
Then I had it come up with 10 brands with strong visual identity and use the Firecrawl MCP to extract the branding from each one
Colors, fonts, typography
All pulled auto-magically
Phase 3: Testing and Fixing ⚙️
This part took the most back and forth.
Some issues I ran into:
Firecrawl only allows 5 concurrent requests, so it had to queue them up.
Generic homepages don't always show the brand well, so I had to find specific blog posts from each site.
Your local Microsoft Word might not have premium fonts installed, so it defaults to Calibri even if the file has the right font specified.
Had to tell Claude Code to update the actual skill file, not just fix things in context.
The takeaway:
→ You can take any existing Claude Code skill and augment it
→ The docx skill becomes a document polisher.
→ The pptx skill could become a deck polisher.
Feed it your client's website, extract their branding, and generate documents that look like theirs.
Zero code written, just API documentation provided and an API key.
Enjoy 🫶

lessons.title: The e-Book Generator System 📕
lessons.description:
If you check out the sample I attached to this post, you'll see it looks pretty polished!
🔗 𝗚𝗶𝘁𝗛𝘂𝗯 𝗥𝗲𝗽𝗼: e-Book Generator System
𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗜 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝘁:
A Claude Code skill that generates polished e-books (DocX to PDF) with AI-generated cover images using 𝗚𝗲𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗶 𝟯'𝘀 𝗡𝗮𝗻𝗼 𝗕𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗻𝗮. Full-bleed cover art, proper text positioning, the whole thing.
Use it for lead magnets, team resources, client deliverables, whatever.
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀:
𝗣𝗵𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝟭 - Reverse Engineering
I grabbed a McKinsey e-book and asked Claude Code: "Can you make something like this?" First few versions looked... rough. High school report energy. So I kept iterating ("make it prettier, make it prettier") until we got somewhere decent.
𝗣𝗵𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝟮 - Adding Image Generation
The body content was fine. The cover page was the problem. So I wired up Gemini 3's Nano Banana API to generate portrait-sized cover images. Abstract, textbook-style visuals that relate to the topic without being too literal.
𝗣𝗵𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝟯 - Positioning and Polish
First attempt: image and text were clashing. Asked it to make the image bleed over the whole page, superimpose the title with a backdrop so it's readable. Worked in one shot. Sometimes things just click.
𝗢𝗻𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗜 𝗻𝗼𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗲𝗱:
My prompts are getting lazier. Not because I don't care, but because these models are finally good enough to read between the lines. Two years ago, I was selling five-page scientific prompts. Now I can say "make it prettier" and it knows what I mean.
We're getting closer to the world I've always wanted: vague request in, polished output out.
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝘁𝗲𝗰𝗵𝗻𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗯𝗶𝘁𝘀:
- Claude Code for DocX/PDF generation (skills I've already shown you)
- Gemini 3 Nano Banana for cover image generation
- YOLO mode in the Cursor extension (video shows how to set this up)
- Compact command to manage context when it gets heavy
𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗺𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀:
Designrr charges monthly for something you can now do yourself
Create branded e-books for your website, your clients, your lead funnels, whatever you need.
Could even combine this with the AI Strategy Factory.
Take those 19 deliverables, package the best ones into a polished e-book with your logo and brand colors, and now you've got something you can actually hand to a client or post on your site.
Pettiness → productivity
Enjoy. 🎁

lessons.title: The n8n Workflow Architect System 🧠
lessons.description:
Before you build anything, you should probably ask: "Should I even be using n8n for this?"
It's no secret I've been using Claude Code heavily. You've seen me use it for almost everything
BUT there are times when n8n is genuinely the better choice. The problem is knowing when.
So I built a system that helps you decide before you write a single node (and to help all the current hackathoners)
It marries the open-source n8n MCP + the out-of-the-box new skills + MY skill I designed for design thinking
🔗 GitHub Repo: n8n Powerhouse Repo
What I built:
A Claude Code skill layer that sits on top of the open source n8n MCP. It acts as a thought partner in plan mode, helping you decide:
- Should you use n8n, Claude Code, or standard Python?
- If n8n, what's the best design structure?
- What's the path of least resistance and why?
The process:
Phase 1: Setting Up the n8n MCP
The open source n8n MCP has gotten way better in the last month. 39 tools, free, connects to your n8n Cloud (or self-hosted instance). One-line command to install it. No more messing with .mcp.json files.
Phase 2: Adding the Existing Skills
The MCP repo now includes skills files for code nodes, design patterns, validation, and more. These help Claude Code understand how to use n8n properly. Cloned the repo, added to the skills directory, done.
Phase 3: Building the Workflow Architect
This is the layer I added. I talked for 20 minutes about my mental model for when to use n8n vs code, then had Claude format it into a skill. It covers:
- The authentication problem (OAuth is annoying in pure code)
- Processing limits and long-running workflows
- The hybrid approach (using n8n as infrastructure within Claude Code)
- When visual workflows make sense for non-technical maintainers
Phase 4: Wiring It All Together
Created a proper .claude folder structure with a claude.md file that understands how all the pieces connect. New sessions automatically know which skills to invoke.
The decision framework:
Quick version from the skill:
- Does it involve OAuth? → Probably n8n
- Will non-developers maintain it? → Probably n8n
- Does it need to wait days or weeks? → Probably n8n
- Is it a one-off script? → Probably Claude Code
You can change this logic. This is my opinion based on the workflows I've seen. Yours might differ.
Why this matters:
Instead of jumping straight into building and realizing halfway through that you picked the wrong tool, you now have a planning step. Go into plan mode, describe your business stack (Shopify, Zoho, Stripe, whatever), and let it recommend the approach before you commit.
In the video, I tested it with an e-commerce workflow. It correctly identified that all four integrations should use n8n because of managed auth and non-technical maintainers.
Then it built the Shopify webhook workflow using the MCP.
Enjoy. 🎁

The MCP repo now includes skills files for code nodes, design patterns, validation, and more. These help Claude Code understand how to use n8n properly. Cloned the repo, added to the skills directory, done.
Phase 3: Building the Workflow Architect
This is the layer I added. I talked for 20 minutes about my mental model for when to use n8n vs code, then had Claude format it into a skill. It covers:
- The authentication problem (OAuth is annoying in pure code)
- Processing limits and long-running workflows
- The hybrid approach (using n8n as infrastructure within Claude Code)
- When visual workflows make sense for non-technical maintainers
Phase 4: Wiring It All Together
Created a proper .claude folder structure with a
claude.md
file that understands how all the pieces connect. New sessions automatically know which skills to invoke.
The decision framework:
Quick version from the skill:
- Does it involve OAuth? → Probably n8n
- Will non-developers maintain it? → Probably n8n
- Does it need to wait days or weeks? → Probably n8n
- Is it a one-off script? → Probably Claude Code
You can change this logic. This is my opinion based on the workflows I've seen. Yours might differ.
Why this matters:

Instead of jumping straight into building and realizing halfway through that you picked the wrong tool, you now have a planning step. Go into plan mode, describe your business stack (Shopify, Zoho, Stripe, whatever), and let it recommend the approach before you commit.
In the video, I tested it with an e-commerce workflow. It correctly identified that all four integrations should use n8n because of managed auth and non-technical maintainers.
Then it built the Shopify webhook workflow using the MCP.
Enjoy. 🎁

lessons.title: The Ultimate MegaRAG System 📚
lessons.description:
This is the last Claude Code system of 2025, and it's probably the best
I think I accidentally rebuilt two SaaS products. Oops 🤷🏽‍♂️
A few months ago, I showed you Ragie, a plug and play RAG as a service tool. Then there's Vectorize, which blew up this year. Both charge monthly. Both are black boxes. You can't control how they chunk. You can't see what's happening under the hood.
So I built my own. And I might have gone a little overboard.
𝗩𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗼 attached showing exactly how I built this over 4-5 days of late nights (12am to 4am, burning the midnight candle). You'll watch me struggle, debug, and figure it out in real time.
Click to the right of the original video when you open this post.
🔗 𝗚𝗶𝘁𝗛𝘂𝗯 𝗥𝗲𝗽𝗼: MegaRag
𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗜 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝘁:
A multimodal RAG system that handles any file type. Drag and drop MP4s, MP3s, PNGs, PDFs, DocX files, text files, all at the same time. It processes them, chunks them, extracts entities, maps relationships, builds knowledge graphs, and lets you query everything through five different search modes.
Think Vectorize, but you own it. Think Ragie, but no black box (and monthly fee).
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝗲𝗮𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗹𝗶𝘀𝘁:
File Support:
- MP4 videos (frame by frame text extraction)
- MP3 audio (transcription and chunking)
- PNG/images (Gemini vision describes and chunks)
- PDF, DocX, text files (Dockling inspired parsing)
Five Querying Modes:
- Mix: The full picture. Chunks + entities + relationships
- Hybrid: Entity search combined with relationship search
- Local: Find specific entities (people, companies, places)
- Global: Explore connections (how is X related to Y)
- Naive: Classic semantic similarity search
The Interface:
- Chat with persistent history and citations
- Source references with relevance ranking
- Data explorer with chunk viewer
- Entity browser across all documents
- Knowledge graph visualization (basic, but functional)
- Admin panel with dashboard and stats
- Dark mode (obviously)
The API:
- Document upload endpoint
- Query endpoint with all five modes
- Chat endpoint
- Document listing endpoint
- Ready for n8n, Claude Code workflows, or your own MCP server
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀:
𝗣𝗵𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝟬 - The Lazy Genius Move
This is the sauce. I cloned four open source repos into my Claude Code environment: Dockling, LightRAG, RAG Anything, and Video RAG. I didn't use them directly. I wanted Claude Code to draw inspiration from what already works and combine the best ideas into something new.
Then I ran /init and said: "Create a claude.md with your understanding of all these repos."
Now Claude had a comprehensive mental model of multimodal RAG before we wrote a single line of code.
𝗣𝗵𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝟭 - Supabase Setup
I set up the Supabase MCP. It's one of the few MCPs I still use. My old reliable. $10/month, handles everything: edge functions, queries, tables, PGVector for embeddings. All the dirty work.
𝗣𝗵𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝟮 - File Processing Lanes
Each file type gets its own processing lane:
Lane 1 (Text): File read → token chunking → stored. Done.
Lane 2 (Documents): PDF/DocX → Dockling parser → text blocks + tables → Gemini describes tables → chunking → embeddings.
Lane 3 (Images): Gemini Vision describes the image → chunk the description → embeddings.
Lane 4 (Video): Upload to Gemini File API → wait for processing → frame by frame extraction → chunking.
Lane 5 (Audio): Gemini File API → transcription → chunking.
𝗣𝗵𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝟯 - Entity Extraction and Knowledge Graphs
Every chunk gets analyzed for entities (people, places, things, concepts). Entities get categorized under subjects. Relationships get mapped between entities. This is what powers the advanced search modes.
My knowledge graph visualization is basic. You could make it way better. But it works and shows you how everything connects.
𝗣𝗵𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝟰 - The Five Query Modes
Naive mode: Generate embedding → search chunks → return top 5. Fast, but shallow.
Mix mode (default): Generate embedding → search chunks → search entities → search relationships → find related chunks → deduplicate → return with citations. Slower, but comprehensive.
The other three modes fall somewhere in between depending on what you need.
𝗣𝗵𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝟱 - Chat Interface and Admin Panel
Built chat with persistent history, source citations with relevance scores, and clickable references so you can trace exactly where each answer came from.
Admin panel gives you document stats, entity distribution, recent uploads, and the knowledge graph explorer.
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝘁𝗲𝗰𝗵 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗰𝗸:
All you need is Supabase and a Gemini API key. That's it.
- Frontend: NextJS, React, TypeScript
- Backend: NextJS, Supabase, Dockling (inspiration), FastAPI
- Embeddings: Gemini 2.0 (cheap and works)
- Storage: Supabase storage + Postgres with PGVector
- Processing: Gemini File API for video/audio
I tried to reduce how many things you need to sign up for. Two services. Done.
𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗺𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀:
I'm going to say something that might be controversial. The way I see 2026 and forward, I don't see many use cases where you should use no-code tools for RAG anymore.
RAG changes so much. RAG, if you want to make it world class, takes many layers. Whether it's Claude Code or Windsurf or Cursor or whatever IDE, I don't think RAG should be done in no-code workflows anymore. And I'm gonna stand by that statement.
This flexibility of building such a sophisticated system would take you ages in n8n. It took me 4-5 days of late nights. But it was doable and I didn't actually write any code myself. I entered a couple API keys in the database secrets, but that's about it.
𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗱𝗼 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀:
- White label it for clients
- Add a preprocessing pipeline
- Turn it into an MCP server
- Plug the API into n8n or Claude Code workflows
- Build on the knowledge graph visualization
- Make it from good to awesome
Is this perfect? No. I haven't battle tested this in production to the point where I can say I just killed a multi-billion dollar industry. But I made a dent. And you can take what I built and find all the bugs and make it infinitely better.

lessons.title: Notebook LM Re-Imagined 📓
lessons.description:
I rebuilt Google's NotebookLM from scratch using Claude Code - but made it actually useful for power users.
What it does:
- RAG-powered chat with your documents (PDFs, DOCX, websites, YouTube)
- Multi-person podcast generation (deep dive, brief, debate modes)
- Video explainers via Alibaba's Wan 2.5 (10x cheaper than Veo)
- Deep research mode using Gemini's research API
- Study materials: flashcards, quizzes, study guides, FAQs
- Slide decks, reports, data tables - all exportable
- Full REST API with 50 endpoints - use it from n8n, Zapier, anywhere
The key difference: Everything is API-first. The web UI is just another client. You own the infrastructure.
Tech stack:
- Supabase (database, auth, storage)
- Vercel (hosting)
- Gemini API (RAG, TTS, research)
- FastAPI backend + Next.js frontend
In the repo you'll find:
- Complete codebase (frontend + backend)
- 3 PRD documents (Vision, Spec, Implementation Guide)
- 28 architecture diagrams
- 8 prompt templates for each build phase
GitHub: NotebookLM Reimagined
Watch the full build walkthrough on my channel if you want to see how it all comes together.

lessons.title: 1) Getting Started & Environment Setup
lessons.description:
GitHub Repo: https://github.com/AllCytes/cc-fundamentals-01-getting-started
Alright so this is where it all starts. We're gonna get Claude Code installed, set up your environment, and make sure everything is runnin' smooth. The big thing I teach here is what I call the "brilliant but blind" principle  - basically Claude is insanely capable, but it's only as good as the context you give it. So we cover how to structure your project, manage your API keys safely, and set things up so Claude actually understands what you're workin' with.
What You'll Learn:
How to install and verify Claude Code on your machine
Why project structure matters (and how it affects Claude's output)
Managing API keys the right way so you don't accidentally expose them
Setting up your first project with the proper folder structure
The mental model behind how Claude Code actually thinks
Key Takeaway: Think of Claude Code like having a senior dev on your team  - but you gotta give it the right context first. This module shows you exactly how to do that.

lessons.title: 2) Slash Commands
lessons.description:
GitHub Repo: https://github.com/AllCytes/cc-fundamentals-02-commands
Commands are one of the biggest game changers in Claude Code. Instead of typing out the same instructions every single time, you save them as a slash command and reuse them whenever you want. I'm talkin' one-click workflows that you build once and use forever. This module teaches you how to create, organize, and use custom commands from scratch.
What You'll Learn:
What slash commands are and why they're a huge time-saver
How to create your own custom commands from scratch
The template pattern that keeps your results consistent
How to install commands globally so they work across all your projects
9 production-ready commands are included in the repo so you can start usin' them right awayKey Takeaway: Once you start using commands, you're never gonna go back to manually typing out the same prompts over and over. Trust me on this one.

lessons.title: 3) The Core Workflow
lessons.description:
GitHub Repo: https://github.com/AllCytes/cc-fundamentals-03-core-workflow
This is honestly the most important module in the entire course. You're gonna learn the 5-phase workflow that takes Claude Code from "just a chatbot" to a legit production-ready development partner: Plan → Build → Validate → Review → Commit. Whether you're fixin' a quick bug or buildin' out a full feature, this workflow keeps everything organized and your code quality high.
What You'll Learn:
The 5-phase workflow: Plan, Build, Validate, Review, Commit
How to use spec files to track what you're building and why
Three workflow recipes depending on the situation: Quick Fix, Standard Feature, and Full Workflow
Visual verification with Playwright (Claude can actually see your app!)
How the specs folder system works for tracking your progress
Key Takeaway: This workflow is the difference between vaguely askin' Claude for help and consistently shipping quality work. It's how you go from amateur to professional use of Claude Code.

lessons.title: 4) MCPs (Model Context Protocol)
lessons.description:
GitHub Repo: https://github.com/AllCytes/cc-fundamentals-04-mcp
MCPs (Model Context Protocol servers) are what give Claude Code superpowers. They let Claude interact with databases, browsers, APIs, and external services  - way beyond just reading and writing files. This module covers what MCPs are, how to install them, how to evaluate whether they're safe to use, and you'll even build your own simple ones
What You'll Learn:
What MCPs are and the three capabilities they bring to the table (Tools, Resources, Prompts)
How to install and configure MCPs for your projects
Security evaluation: how to tell if an MCP is legit and safe
Three custom MCPs included in the repo: a memory system, a prompt library, and a work journal
Recommended MCPs for common use cases like Playwright, Supabase, Notion, and SlackKey Takeaway: MCPs are how you take Claude Code from a code assistant to a full-on automation platform. Think of them as plugins that let Claude talk to pretty much anything.

lessons.title: 5) Skills
lessons.description:
GitHub Repo: https://github.com/AllCytes/cc-fundamentals-05-skills
Skills are the next level up from commands. Commands are single-file prompts, but skills are full multi-file packages that combine instructions, templates, and even MCPs into seriously powerful, reusable workflows. This module shows you how to use existing skills and create your own  - we're talkin' generating documents, extracting data, automating complex stuff, all that.
What You'll Learn:
The difference between commands and skills (and when to use each one)
How skills are actually structured under the hood
5 production-ready skills included: File Factory (creates PPTX, DOCX, XLSX, PDF), Video Transcript Extractor, Time Travel (git checkpoints), MCP Builder, and Skill Creator
A showcase folder with 63 example outputs so you can see what these skills actually produce
Access to 21,000+ community-built skills you can plug in
Key Takeaway: Skills let you package up complex workflows into something anyone can trigger with a single command. They're how you scale your Claude Code setup across a team.

5 production-ready skills included: File Factory (creates PPTX, DOCX, XLSX, PDF), Video Transcript Extractor, Time Travel (git checkpoints), MCP Builder, and Skill Creator

Access to 21,000+ community-built skills you can plug in

Subagents are where things get really cool. You can have Claude spin up specialized workers for specific tasks  - a code reviewer, a test runner, a doc generator  - all runnin' independently without losing track of the main work. Key Takeaway: Subagents are like having a team of specialists on call. Instead of one agent tryin' to do everything, you delegate tasks to purpose-built agents that each do one thing really well.

You'll set up three protection tiers that keep your projects safe without slowin' you down.

What hooks are and how they protect your work (PreToolUse and PostToolUse)
Three protection tiers: Zero Access, Read Only, and No Delete

A complete Security Audit skill with quick checks and full audits
Key Takeaway: Security isn't optional  - it's table stakes. The beauty of these hooks is they run automatically in the background, so you get protection without even having to think about it.

lessons.title: Mark's Harness 🪂
lessons.description:
My daily-driver setup for running the pi coding agent 100% locally. No cloud model, no API bill, no internet required. It runs Qwen3.5 122B through LM Studio on a MacBook, and the harness is the reason a local model can one-shot complete, verified websites headlessly instead of flailing.
Repo → https://github.com/earlyaidopters/marks-pi-harness
What you get
14 extensions that make a local model reliable. The big one is browser_check, which screenshots the page and forces the model to look at its own work and rule PASS or FAIL. Plus gates it cannot talk past, offline detection, context caps, and a skill router.
Website-building skills. Two complete systems, one for cinematic 3D scroll sites, one for premium editorial sites, each with battle-tested starter templates. A local 122B has built full production sites through them with zero tool errors.
Session memory. Handoff and prime skills so the agent picks up exactly where the last session ended.
The rulebook. An AGENTS.md distilled from real failures. Every rule in it bit me first.Get it
git clone https://github.com/earlyaidopters/marks-pi-harness.gitcd marks-pi-harnessThen drop the contents into ~/.pi/agent/, run npm install there, and point models.json at whatever vision-capable model you run in LM Studio. Full setup steps are in the repo README.
Stay current
I push improvements as the harness evolves. To pull the latest,
cd marks-pi-harnessgit pullthen copy the updated files into ~/.pi/agent/ again and restart pi (it loads extensions and skills at startup, so a running session will not see changes).
Watch for upgrades
On the repo page, hit Watch → Custom → Releases and Discussions, or just Watch → All activity to get every commit. The Star button helps too, but Watch is what actually notifies you.
Or from the terminal with the GitHub CLI,
gh repo view earlyaidopters/marks-pi-harness --webgh api -X PUT /repos/earlyaidopters/marks-pi-harness/subscription -f subscribed=trueWhy bother
Frontier cloud models tolerate sloppy setups. Local models do not. The gap between "local models are toys" and "a 122B just shipped my landing page while I made coffee" is not the model. It is the harness around it.

lessons.title: ⚠️ DISCLAIMERS
lessons.description:
Read this before you stand anything up. ClaudeClaw Enterprise OS is a V0. It is a blueprint and a learning tool, not a turnkey product, and it is not built for personal use.
🧪 This is v1
This is the first version. There are rough edges in every tab and in how each one was designed.
The goal was to show what a full enterprise agent operating system could look like on AWS, not to ship a finished product.
Treat it as a foundation you study and adapt, not a polished app you flip on.🚫 This is not for personal use
If you set this up just to play, you will spend hundreds of dollars to make it exist, before you have even used it. For almost everyone here, the right move is to watch the walkthroughs, audit the GitHub repo with Claude Code or Codex, and absorb the mental models. That is where the real value lives.
If you want a personal agent, ClaudeClaw, Hermes, or open claw on Railway or a similar host is far cheaper and far simpler. This is a completely different beast.
💸 What it actually costs
• Standing up the infrastructure alone runs into the hundreds of dollars, with little or no inference.
• A realistic floor for running it for a month is roughly $300 to $400, and that is after squeezing it down.
• Left on for a month, you can easily spend double the cost of this community membership just to tinker.
• The first month of building this came in around $800.
🧾 Why the bill adds up
• AWS meters most things by the hour, the same way a utility bill meters electricity, gas, and water.
• The meter runs even with zero users. Once the infrastructure is up, you pay whether or not anyone messages your agent. That is unlike Vercel or Railway free tiers.
• A staging environment plus a production environment means you pay for two full copies of the same infrastructure.
• Deploys are slow, often 15 to 30 minutes each, so a three hour build can stretch into seven once you add the redeploys and checks.
🛡️ How to protect yourself
• Set a hard daily spend cap in AWS so a runaway process cannot drain your account.
• Turn on multi factor authentication. A compromised AWS account can become a very expensive bill.
• Do not run your agent in YOLO or bypass permissions mode. Babysit it. Approve each step and question anything you do not understand.
• Ask Claude Code or Codex to sweep for abandoned services you spun up by accident and are paying for but not using.
• Plan first. Run the build in plan mode, get a cost estimate, and make peace with the monthly number before you deploy.
🎯 What this is really for
• Awareness. Understand what building a system like this involves, so you can speak to it with confidence.
• Advisory. Be the solution architect who hands a company a roadmap, not the person who foots the bill.
• A real client use case. Only stand it up end to end if a client or a firm need genuinely justifies it.
There is no honor in spending the money just to set it up and tear it down a day later. This is not your substitute for ClaudeClaw.
🔒 Security and compliance reality
• This is not Fort Knox. It is not perfect security and it is not a perfect experience.
• As it stands it is not fully SOC 2 or HIPAA compliant. It gives you the foundation and a pathway to start those conversations, nothing more.
• Getting to truly compliant takes an IT team, human oversight, and real work on your side, tuned to your region, your domain, and your organization.
Bottom line. Enjoy the walkthroughs, study the code, take the knowledge. Only go further if the use case truly demands it and you fully understand what you are signing up to pay.

lessons.title: TIPS ON HOW TO INSTALL 💡
lessons.description:
1) Create a brand new AWS account at https://aws.amazon.com. Use a fresh email address, add a payment card, and finish the phone verification. It must be a standalone account that is only for this, not your company's existing account. Activation can take from a few minutes up to an hour, so do this step first and keep going while you wait.
2) Install the AWS CLI (the tool that lets your computer talk to AWS). Mac users with Homebrew type "brew install awscli" in Terminal. Everyone else, download it from https://aws.amazon.com/cli. To confirm it worked, type "aws --version" in your terminal and you should see a version number.
3) Install Node.js version 20 or newer from https://nodejs.org (pick the LTS download). Confirm with "node --version" in your terminal.
4) Install git if you do not already have it. Mac users, just type "git --version" in Terminal and macOS will offer to install it for you. Windows users, download it from https://git-scm.com.
5) Connect your terminal to your new AWS account. Type "aws configure" and paste in the access key and secret key from your AWS account (in the AWS website, click your name top right, then Security credentials, then Create access key). Prove it worked by typing "aws sts get-caller-identity". If that prints your account number, you are connected.
6) Grant Claude model access in AWS. In the AWS website, search for "Bedrock", open it, click "Model access" in the left menu, and request access to the Anthropic Claude models. Approval usually takes a few minutes. You can skip this step for now if you want, the installer will notice, show you the exact link, and wait for you.
7) Get your personal download command from this page. https://claudeclaw-token-server.steep-water-fa9f.workers.dev/enterprise. Click Copy on the box at the top. This command contains a temporary access key that expires in about an hour, so if you take a break, just reload that page for a fresh one.
8) Paste that command into your terminal and press Enter. It downloads everything into a folder called "claudeclaw-enterprise". If you have installed before and want the latest version, delete your old folder first, then paste again.
9) Move into the folder and install its dependencies. Type these two lines, pressing Enter after each.
cd claudeclaw-enterprise
npm ci --ignore-scripts
The second one takes about two minutes.
10) Now choose your path. EASY PATH. Type "npm run up" and press Enter. That single command runs everything. A short setup wizard (pick the cheapest tier and "infra-only" mode if you are unsure), free safety checks, a test message to Claude, the real deploy (15 to 30 minutes), and a final verification. Whenever something needs a click from you, like the Claude access from step 6, it prints the exact link, waits for you to do it, and then continues on its own. No Docker on your machine? Not a problem, the installer notices and builds the app inside your AWS account instead (a few cents, about 10 extra minutes). You can press Ctrl-C at any time and run "npm run up" again later, it picks up where it left off.
11) AI AGENT PATH. If you use Claude Code or another AI coding agent, open it inside the "claudeclaw-enterprise" folder and say "install this". The agent reads the AGENTS.md file in the folder and drives the exact same steps for you, and it will walk you through steps 5 and 6 if you have not done them. If your agent wants more detail, point it at README.md (the "Start here" table at the top) and docs/agent-setup.md (the full step-by-step runbook written for agents).
12) The last few clicks. When it finishes, it prints a checklist of the few one-time clicks left. The two that matter most. Click the confirmation link AWS emails you (so alerts can reach you), and open your dashboard using the DASHBOARD_URL and DASHBOARD_TOKEN it printed. That dashboard is your Mission Control for everything.
13) Two commands worth knowing afterward. "npm run power:setup" gives you a pause button that drops the bill to a floor while you are not using it. "npm run destroy" removes absolutely everything from your AWS account if you want out, and proves the account is clean.
Stuck on any step? The docs/troubleshooting.md file in the folder explains every check and its exact fix, or ask in the community with a screenshot of the error.

at
https://aws.amazon.com

. Use a fresh email address, add a payment card, and finish the phone verification. It must be a standalone account that is only for this, not your company's existing account. Activation can take from a few minutes up to an hour, so do this step first and keep going while you wait.
Install the AWS CLI
(the tool that lets your computer talk to AWS). Mac users with Homebrew type "brew install awscli" in Terminal. Everyone else, download it from
https://aws.amazon.com/cli
. To confirm it worked, type "aws --version" in your terminal and you should see a version number.
Install Node.js version 20 or newer
from
https://nodejs.org
(pick the LTS download). Confirm with "node --version" in your terminal.
Install git
if you do not already have it. Mac users, just type "git --version" in Terminal and macOS will offer to install it for you. Windows users, download it from
https://git-scm.com
Connect your terminal to your new AWS account.

Type "aws configure" and paste in the access key and secret key from your AWS account (in the AWS website, click your name top right, then Security credentials, then Create access key). Prove it worked by typing "aws sts get-caller-identity". If that prints your account number, you are connected.
Grant Claude model access in AWS.

In the AWS website, search for "Bedrock", open it, click "Model access" in the left menu, and request access to the Anthropic Claude models. Approval usually takes a few minutes. You can skip this step for now if you want, the installer will notice, show you the exact link, and wait for you.
Get your personal download command from this page.
https://claudeclaw-token-server.steep-water-fa9f.workers.dev/enterprise
. Click Copy on the box at the top. This command contains a temporary access key that expires in about an hour, so if you take a break, just reload that page for a fresh one.
Paste that command into your terminal
and press Enter. It downloads everything into a folder called "claudeclaw-enterprise". If you have installed before and want the latest version, delete your old folder first, then paste again.
Move into the folder and install its dependencies.
Type these two lines, pressing Enter after each.
cd claudeclaw-enterprise
npm ci --ignore-scripts
The second one takes about two minutes.
Now choose your path.
E
ASY PATH.

Type "npm run up" and press Enter. That single command runs everything. A short setup wizard (pick the cheapest tier and "infra-only" mode if you are unsure), free safety checks, a test message to Claude, the real deploy (15 to 30 minutes), and a final verification. Whenever something needs a click from you, like the Claude access from step 6, it prints the exact link, waits for you to do it, and then continues on its own. No Docker on your machine? Not a problem, the installer notices and builds the app inside your AWS account instead (a few cents, about 10 extra minutes). You can press Ctrl-C at any time and run "npm run up" again later, it picks up where it left off.
AI AGENT PATH.
If you use Claude Code or another AI coding agent, open it inside the "claudeclaw-enterprise" folder and say "install this". The agent reads the
AGENTS.md
file in the folder and drives the exact same steps for you, and it will walk you through steps 5 and 6 if you have not done them. If your agent wants more detail, point it at
README.md
(the "Start here" table at the top) and docs/
agent-setup.md
(the full step-by-step runbook written for agents).
The last few clicks.

When it finishes, it prints a checklist of the few one-time clicks left. The two that matter most. Click the confirmation link AWS emails you (so alerts can reach you), and open your dashboard using the DASHBOARD_URL and DASHBOARD_TOKEN it printed. That dashboard is your Mission Control for everything.
Two commands worth knowing afterward.

"npm run power:setup" gives you a pause button that drops the bill to a floor while you are not using it. "npm run destroy" removes absolutely everything from your AWS account if you want out, and proves the account is clean.
Stuck on any step? The docs/
troubleshooting.md
file in the folder explains every check and its exact fix, or ask in the community with a screenshot of the error.

lessons.title: Beginner's Corner - June 29
lessons.description:
Check out our Beginner's Corner resource →

📝 Meeting Summary:

---

---
🧭 1. The session was designed as an interactive beginner workshop, not a lecture
The facilitator opened by making it clear that the call works best when people participate, turn on their cameras if possible, and ask direct questions. The goal was to understand each person’s level with Claude Code so the session could be tailored in real time instead of becoming a one-way presentation.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
🗂️ 2. Claude Code organization starts with clear project folders and layered CLAUDE.md files
A major teaching point was how to structure work across multiple companies or projects. The explanation was that users can keep one global CLAUDE.md file, then create project-specific folders with their own CLAUDE.md files that override the broader rules as needed, creating a nested “Russian dolls” style of context management.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
⚙️ 3. Commands and skills serve different purposes, and skills should stay lean and reusable
A strong section focused on the difference between slash commands and skills. Commands were framed as manual shortcuts, while skills were described as reusable workflows that Claude can trigger more intelligently. The facilitator also stressed that imported skills should be reviewed and adapted rather than used blindly, because many are too bloated and should be simplified for the user’s own system.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
📚 4. The best way to learn Claude Code is to build something real while using the course as support
The guidance was not to passively watch lessons and hope understanding appears later. Instead, participants were encouraged to pick a real project for their business or life, start experimenting immediately, make mistakes, and then use the community courses to understand what they are experiencing. The core message was that hands-on use creates much stronger learning than abstract study.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
🚀 5. Claude becomes far more useful when applied to a specific workflow instead of vague experimentation
Toward the end, the conversation moved into how to use Claude for practical outputs like training content, multilingual scripts, and personalized voice-based material. The broader takeaway was that once someone knows the workflow they want, Claude can help design the structure, extract patterns from prior work, and turn scattered material into a more repeatable system.

lessons.title: Beginner's Corner - July 14
lessons.description:
Check out our Beginner's Corner resource →

📝 Meeting Summary:

---

---
🧭 1. The session was framed as a hands-on beginner workshop where questions are the point Alexandra opened by inviting people to turn on cameras and interrupt freely, stressing there are no dumb questions and that everyone is a beginner in something. She checked the room's experience level (from total beginners to people with a bit of no-code app experience) so she could pace the teaching around real questions rather than deliver a one-way lecture.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
🧠 2. Good context is the foundation — feed Claude the right information, not everything The core metaphor was a garden: Claude is flexible and knowledgeable, but without your specific context it will "hallucinate" (invent answers), and if you dump too much on it, you blow the context window and it drowns in information. The skill is architecting your data — giving Claude a well-organized library it consults only when needed, not forcing it to read every book before it can bring you a coffee.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
🗂️ 3. CLAUDE.md is your instructions to Claude, layered like Russian dolls CLAUDE.md is a plain-text file Claude reads at the start of every session — your ID card: who you are, your tone, your language, your business, house rules. There's a global one (loaded in every conversation, so keep it minimal) plus project- and subfolder-level files that override it depending on where you're working. Keep it short (aim ~50 lines), write it for the agent not for humans (that's what a README is for), and only include durable, non-obvious things. Before adding a rule, ask Claude if it already knows it — if it's default behavior (e.g. "write tests," "use types"), leave it out; it's just noise.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
🌱 4. Progressive disclosure keeps context lean via a rules/ folder with front matter paths Anything in your main CLAUDE.md loads every session and costs attention. The fix: move situational rules into a rules/ folder where each rule file has front matter specifying a path — the rule stays asleep and only wakes when Claude touches a matching file type (e.g. .md files inside your content folder). Key warning confirmed live via the Claude Code Guide agent: a rule with no path loads every single session anyway, there's no cache — files are read fresh from disk each session/compaction — and you don't need to memorize the syntax because Claude writes the front matter for you.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
📌 5. Memory is the second system — the notes Claude keeps about you on its own Distinct from CLAUDE.md (which you write), the memory system is Claude's own set of "post-its" — a memory.md index plus topic files it creates from what it learns across conversations. The index opens every session; topic files open only when relevant. Analogy used: the movie Memento — Claude's "brain isn't connected to its mouth," so it writes itself notes to persist knowledge. You can inspect these with /memory, but you generally don't author them yourself.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
💬 6. Clarifying the big confusion: "Claude Code" is not about coding A newcomer's question prompted an important clarification — Claude Code is a poorly-named product: it's about talking to Claude (the LLM) through an agentic editing harness, not about writing code. You can use it for marketing, copywriting, organizing an Obsidian second brain, building a knowledge business — anything. (Example raised: Bernadette wants to organize thousands of health/nutrition files into a sellable second brain; the same CLAUDE.md + rules + memory principles apply.) Side tangent on tooling: Alexandra prefers Warp (a terminal with superpowers — tabs, pinned projects, file tree, its own agent) over the basic terminal or the desktop app, since Claude ultimately "lives in the terminal."
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
🧹 7. Next week: build a "garden maintenance" audit skill together Gardens grow weeds — broken links to renamed/deleted files, rules that quietly stopped loading, stale deadlines ("next Monday" six months ago), index/memory mismatches, bloated files near their size limit. The plan is to build a lean audit skill that reads and reports only (never auto-fixes), outputs a 30-second scannable report, and gets scheduled to run weekly. Matt shared his own working maintenance skill as a starting point, and Claude's advice was telling: build a thin "conductor," not new checkers, since most checks already exist in a mature setup. Guidance for participants: start a skill as a tiny seed (e.g. "flag skills untouched in 14 days") and grow it whenever you find yourself repeating an instruction.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
🦴 8. Bonus: the "caveman" skill and a note on Opus 4.8 verbosity Alexandra shared that Opus 4.8 tends to be verbose (great for copywriting, less ideal for coding or teaching, where she now often switches to 4.7). Her fix is a "caveman" skill with dial-able levels that strips Claude's replies down to terse, to-the-point output with no niceties.
Next session: Monday, 1 PM Eastern. Homework: digest this material, try it on your own setup, and attempt to build the maintenance skill yourself — bring ideas to build on together.

lessons.title: Beginner's Corner - July 21
lessons.description:
Check out our Beginner's Corner resource →

📝 Meeting Summary:

---

---
🧭 1. This session built on the last one — from "planting the garden" to finding "what died in it" Alexandra opened by recapping that the previous session covered CLAUDE.md and the two memory types (the memory system and memory.md, which Claude writes itself). The goal today was to go deeper on skills and build a first real one — a "garden check" audit skill — since the more skills, projects, and files you accumulate, the more your "Claude garden" fills with weeds that quietly break things without warning you. (Beginner materials are now posted on the community website's "Beginners Corner," linked in the last announcement.)
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
🚪 2. A skill is the fourth "container" — and what makes it unique is who decides when it loads All four context tools are Markdown files with front matter; the difference is the trigger. CLAUDE.md loads every session (keep it short). Rules load when you touch a file matching the path in their front matter. memory.md is written by Claude when it judges something relevant. A skill loads when your request matches its description. Key distinction: a skill is not a slash command — a command fires when you type /name, while a skill decides on its own by matching your wording against its description. If you can write a rule, you can write a skill.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
🔔 3. The description is the "doorbell" — the most important and most misunderstood part A skill is one folder + one root file (it can hold more). A myth she debunked (after having Claude dig the docs): the name field in front matter is optional — it's just the listing label. The folder name is what becomes the /command, not the name field. The front matter (name + description) is read all the time for every installed skill, so it costs context permanently — one skill is fine, but 60 skills rot your context. The body below the dashes only loads if the skill fires. Critical trap: a vague description never throws an error, it just silently never fires — you think the skill is broken when it's only "muted." So the description must contain the actual words you'd say. Practical cautions: don't write in multiple languages (English only, even if you talk to Claude in French), never use a colon in front matter (it breaks parsing), and descriptions get cut off after ~1,536 characters.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
⚙️ 4. New territory even for the facilitator: controlling who can invoke a skill and how much Claude sees Two independent questions: who can invoke it (you, Claude, or both) and how much Claude sees (name + description, name only, or nothing). The easy way is the /skills menu — you can cycle a skill between name-only, user-only, and off, and use /context to see what your skills are actually costing. Deeper, front-matter-level control (things Alexandra openly admitted she was learning live):
disable-model-invocation: true — removes the skill from Claude's auto-selection so it won't fire on its own, but you can still run it via /name or have another skill call it. Ideal for deliberate actions (deploy, publish, send invoices) and for helper skills only ever called by other skills.
user-invocable: false — the mirror image: Claude can load it automatically, but you can't type it as a command. Good for background/context skills (e.g. a "legacy architecture" explainer).

📂 5. Progressive disclosure in skills works differently than in CLAUDE.md Skills have no rule folder. Instead, you keep the body lean and link extra material (rubrics, workflows, templates) as plain Markdown links in the body, with a note on when to open each — Claude only reads a linked file when the body tells it to. The danger: a file nothing links to is invisible — Claude won't go looking. So if you split a skill and forget the link, you've silently deleted half of it. Rule of thumb: keep it as short as possible (the docs say under 500 lines, but she considers even that too long), and push everything non-essential into linked files or subfolders. She uses her own rewritten skill-creator (adapted from Anthropic's, which she found too long and buggy) to author skills — she never writes them by hand, only revises.
