- Fixed or variable interest rate (important because especially in today's economy, if you have a variable and all of a sudden interest rates shoot up and inflation shoots up, you can be cooked if it's a loan that's a big amount and you're not expected to be able to pay a new principal amount)
The most important column - The target variable:
We have this very important column. This is the most important column. If you run machine learning, you need what we said before: a target variable.
What is the variable that you're going to hide from the algorithm to run predictions on to see whether or not you can understand and build a model that's better at understanding when someone should be approved?
Basically the model will train anytime you see a one. This is someone who had this profile and was approved for a mortgage.
We could make this a multi-class: Did they get approved and did they end up defaulting on that mortgage that they were approved for? We can make this a lot more complex, but just for simplicity, let's assume one is they just got approved for this mortgage.
We're going to hide this for training and then we're going to use it in testing.
File #2 - The goal.md file:
This is something I put together with AI. All I did was give this file and the CSV and I just did /init in Claude Code.
Here we have the AI agent goal: To build and package a solid mortgage approval ML model.
Using the dataset mortgage_application.csv, build, evaluate, and package a robust binary classification (binary again is just predicting on one single target variable, which we mentioned before, which is whether or not they're approved) that predicts whether a mortgage application should be approved (approved = 1) or rejected (approved = 0).
Deliver a ready-to-use local artifact plus a simple interface that an app can call to run what-if scenarios and return:
- Predicted approval probability
- Binary decision (approval/reject with a configurable threshold)
- Top five features contributing to that decision
This was really important. That's why you were able to see not just the prediction and the percentage but anything that contributed to that as well.
The dataset and target: This is the target variable right here. Although if you gave it the dataset, it would be smart enough to understand what is the target variable. But in this case I had AI build this form so I could spoon feed it.
In terms of the features: This is something that Claude or whatever model was smart enough to figure out nowadays: What is each type of data? Is it numeric or is it categorical? It can ingest the whole file so I didn't need to do this.
The AI walks through the steps:
Step 1: Load the data, do some basic checks
Step 2: Split the data out. If you remember from one of the lectures, you talked about:
- Training data (where you hide the target variable and have the ML model try and understand and extrapolate how these behave and how it can run predictions to get to the outcome)
- Validation data (a side dataset to validate whether or not your training is going well)
- Test data (the real world, completely unseen data)
Deliverables: These are the variables that you generate when you run a machine learning model.
The preprocessing pipeline: One of the most important things in machine learning is data transformation. How do you clean your data or add new columns in a way that it's easy for it to be translated and ingested by the machine learning algorithm?
Instructions include:
- Impute missing values (if you have nulls or not applicable anywhere, accommodate for that)
- Consider transformation (if the dataset is highly skewed, do some stuff to adjust for that - this is more of an advanced topic)
SMOTE explained: When you have a very imbalanced dataset, good examples are again the cancer dataset where 1-5% might have a diagnosis while 90+ don't.
There's different ways that you can amplify the signal of the ones that do have it. SMOTE in plain English is you synthetically increase the number of examples for the imbalance class.
In this case, the number of people that would be diagnosed to really amplify the signal of what the machine learning model should look for.
Because if it's so imbalanced and you're looking to predict this little diamond in the rough and you have one piece of light amongst a bunch of darkness, really hard for math to do its thing and generalize well.
Model selection: I told it go through a baseline linear model (logistic regression, I reviewed that in day one and day two).
Hyperparameter tuning: This is basically of all the parameters and levers that you can adjust in a particular model. Each model has different ones.
If you dig in you'll see that you have different parameters that you can tune (that's what it's called tuning) and adjust to try and get it to focus better or to not over-index on things.
Deep learning warning: In the world of deep learning you have like 20+ parameters that you can change so it's overwhelming to do deep learning.
One of the other reasons why I never recommend and why it's not recommended for anyone to jump into the deep end and use a black box deep learning model to run predictions.
Not only is it not explainable, but if you don't know what you're doing, you don't appreciate the math behind deep learning, it's really hard to understand why you're choosing certain activation functions.
Deep learning is a beast of its own and it's really hard to be decent at it even with Claude Code if you have no clue what you're doing.
Evaluation: How to evaluate the test sets and what metrics it should use.
Feature importance and explanation: Trying to understand which parameters in the dataset are of the most importance.
Packaging: In this case I'm telling it right now to just run it locally so I can play with it. I'll worry about production later. Right now I'm not talking about production, I'm mentioning what we want to do right now.
The Claude Code process:
All we had was the goal.md file and the application CSV file.
Once I did this, I then run /init like you've seen me do many times before. This will analyze the code base, it will come up with an understanding, then it reads the goal file, puts everything together, and now it creates this claude.md file with an understanding of both files.
I've primed Claude Code to get ready for this. Now I say: Create a plan to execute this in one shot.
It comes up with a plan. It says it's going to create this file called an IPYNB file. If you saw my videos on Google Colab, you have a .py file (that's a Python file). An IPYNB file is a Python file that is in a Jupyter Notebook fashion. So it's a much more visual Python file.
It has markdown, it has explanations as to what's happening in the code itself. Let's say fancy Python file if we want to make it clear cut.
Walking through the different phases:
- Web applications
- Documentation and setup
- Final artifacts (a model file, model metadata, the app itself)
- It's going to create its own API using FastAPI
All of this, again, something that would take days to weeks even with someone that was an intermediate to advanced practitioner. Now you can do this really quickly.
It goes through, creates a to-do list, runs all of this beautiful stuff, goes through, creates inference model, then creates an API to use the model.
The first model disaster:
Let me tell you, the first model it came up with was garbage.
It basically predicted that anyone, no matter how good the credit score, even if they were rocking a million dollars and zero debt and perfect credit score, would get rejected.
I could tell right away that was a flawed model. That's why this is a very iterative process.
It comes up finally with this implementation. Then I tell it: Okay cool, you came up with the implementation, please run it because it tells you here how to use it and how to access it.
I just told it: Well you have access to bash which is the ability to control my computer. I can't see it on localhost, it's an easy issue.
Eventually it runs it and it tells me: All you have to do now is train the model on the data.
I'm like okay well you do it. "You train it" - you can see how sassy I am. I tried to do this on purpose to show you how easy it could be without me going fancy on the prompting.
I could go fancy on the prompting. I could spin up a couple sub-agents to run each part of this training process in parallel. I can really flex in terms of my ability to make this faster and easier, but I just wanted to show you how easy you could do it with minimal understanding of ML principles.
The training process:
Now it updates everything, it runs the training script. It's training on a portion of the data, typically 50-60% of the dataset.
Of 10,000 rows of training from the applications I showed you, it will take around 5-6,000.
Now it's training on everything, takes a sweet time, and then eventually it comes back with this model.
It lies to my face initially. It says it's trained and then it notices itself that the performance is kind of suspect.
Once I saw that I'm like this is going to be an awful model.
It says it's complete, the approval system is live, it runs on localhost. Then I go and run some predictions and they are absolutely horrific.
Now it says approval probability is 20%, 30%. Eventually I go back and forth and I tell it: Listen, you're predicting everything as negative. Let's retrain the model because it seems like there's some imbalance here.
This is what's happening in between back and forth. You don't have to say there's some imbalance. You just say the results are trash. You could literally say that. You could screenshot: "This is trash. It seems like no matter what I do, people are being predicted as negative or predicted as being rejected."
Diagnosing the problem:
Then I ask it a question: Is the model the best we can do in terms of performance?
Now it goes through, runs the machine learning model on some predictions, it analyzes its own data.
Well well, look at this. It realizes there's a class imbalance in the data: 90% of the 10,000 rows were rejected, only 8% were approved.
Like my cancer example, we have this here. Now it goes through a plan on how to improve this.
The fixes it implemented:
It improved the features: It created brand new fields. It used some of the fields to create new features and now creates a new feature called "financial health" which is kind of like a proxy for a few different fields.
This is what I was referring to in lecture one and two: Sometimes you aren't just constrained by the data you're given to run a machine learning model. You can use those fields to create brand new composite fields that you can use to give the model a better end in terms of its next training steps.
Better hyperparameter tuning: I told you we have parameters for different models. It picked the model and then it was able to play around with the features.
In this case it used XGBoost which I referred to in my last video. When in doubt people use XGBoost. Are there better models? Absolutely, especially now. I saw one the other day that beats XGBoost. But for now we're gonna use that.
Class imbalance handling: It created a balanced weighting for different approvals, it focused more on the minority class.
I mentioned one way you can do this - there's many mathematical ways you can amplify the signal of a smaller class.
Model comparison: This is what it cranked out before. It goes through key findings of improvements in the model. It generates that matrix I showed you last day on false positives and true negatives.
It found out what I said: It basically never predicts approval for anyone before.
Now after going through, you can read through everything it did, it comes up with the new architecture it came up with.
I was able to run its own model which is cool to come up with the bottom line.
Deployment to Modal:
Now I ask the question: What do we have to do to serve this online?
What I used to do is serve it on something like Amazon. You have different ways to serve it on Amazon. One of them is using AWS SageMaker (a bit more expensive, something I wouldn't use as much at least back in the day - it's much cheaper now but not by much).
If you were stuck back in the day and you didn't want to code as much, you would use something like AWS SageMaker or GCP Cloud Run.
It comes up with some examples. The easiest method it recommends is Modal which is the one I'm showing you today.
It is really straightforward once you install everything. It'll show you what the process looks like. Then it'll go through the deployment options.
You'll see the hardest one is the one I used to do which is the AWS, Azure, and GCP. You have different things like Digital Ocean.
Heroku: This one is no longer relevant. Heroku used to be the hero back in the day but nobody, I don't know a single human being that does ML to this day that uses it, but still an option.
Then this is what will happen after deployment. It gives you a full guide. It tells you: Use Modal.
It tells you go and run this, go and install this. As usual I say: Do it yourself please. Can you run all the bash and bring me in when I'm needed?
The Modal installation process:
It tries to do it but it seems like it struggles a bit. One thing I noticed is it was easier for me to use Warp and I just used its commands because Claude was kind of not hallucinating but it said it was installed at the beginning but it wasn't.
I just ran the exact commands you see here: pip install, modal setup, modal deploy.
It finally installs it after I get the right command: python3 -m pip install (if you're on Windows or Linux it might be different for you).
Within five minutes it was able to get it. It told me that I needed to upgrade pip. Pip allows you to install libraries on your computer and other things as well.
Then I can run pip install modal. I follow the instructions. I say modal setup. Then it makes me log in, creating an account.
Once you create an account (again it's free - I think you have $5 for free and if you share something you get $30 for free), it's really cheap to run at scale. You won't use that very quickly. It's not like an LLM.
Then I made my new workspace, I logged in, I had a new token and all this, but it was just me clicking through Modal. Nothing fancy here.
Then I just imported this function that Modal asked me to test out to see whether it works or not. It tells you that authentication is finished successfully. Pretty much I was good from there.
After that point, once I did the bash outside of here in Warp, we were good to go.
Deployment success:
Your app is deployed and live. It gives you the link to what we saw, which was this version.
This is what the app looked like on localhost. This is where I went back and forth and I tested it out. I can run this and get prediction. Finally we have some proof.
Then I said okay cool, let's deploy it. Once we deploy it, we go on here on the app itself. We go on overview. You can see, you can click on this.
You can see Claude made an API for us. This API has a method or a section called /predict. Anytime you see 200 OK, meaning it ran perfectly fine.
You can see performance, you can see how it's going. Most of the time this is super straightforward.
What's awesome is if I go back to here you can see all the times I've ran this. All the predictions, you can see every time the status of how it went. This is pretty standard, there's nothing crazy here.
It tells you how quick it is. This should be blazing fast because this is not some Gen AI reasoning model.
Creating the Vercel frontend:
This is all done. This point we were good to go. This is all live and working.
Now it also creates some docs for me, some API docs as well. It created the file.
Now I asked it curious: Would I be able to hit this API from another app on Vercel now?
I know the answer to this is yes but I wanted to show you this: Now that this API exists and it's hosted on a server and we basically create a zip file or compression of this knowledge understanding from the model, you can now hit it from anywhere you want.
Then it tells me how this would be done, it gives me a bunch of code that I don't need to use.
Then I say just this: Let's create an app just like this one but one I can host on Vercel.
It goes and builds the app that I've been showing you up until now. It makes and rebuilds the entire same UI, everything, as well as the predictions. Then it gives me the location of all the core information.
It runs it and then I basically say: Create a brand new GitHub repo.
This is all I'm saying by the way, nothing else happened. This is all Claude just telling me what it did.
It builds a GitHub repo. Now that I had that repo, all I had to do was go back to Vercel, add new project. Now that I had it committed to GitHub, I just had to click mortgage app import and that was pretty much it.
Because it was able to just code the new API documentation of this.
This is the app ID and you can see it can see basically how to run everything. You can see up until now I've only used 3 cents.
It was able to use the exact API and now you can use this from anywhere.
The bigger picture:
You can have an app with technically 10-15 different ML functions if you wanted. I don't recommend it but you could.
You can make really robust apps where maybe 60% is still Gen AI, maybe natural language stuff, maybe knowledge-based RAG stuff, but you can now add components that are a lot richer, a lot more explainable, things that you have a handle over how they'll perform in the wild.
This is one small sliver of what you can do and how you can go from an idea to something that you can push to production.
You could see here my involvement in this process was minimal.
What I'll do is I will make the two files I used available as well as the GitHub repo to you in case it's helpful to you to see how it was built, how it's structured.
You can copy the way I mimicked it. But outside of that you can see that there was minimal intervention from me, prompting it very smart and nerdy things.
The unfair advantage:
This goes from something run on Modal (the platform that hosts machine learning models after training) and then we can actually integrate it in whatever app we want.
That gives us flexibility and it will give you a different edge, especially when you go out in the world and you build vibe-coded apps.
Natural language stuff is now gonna be the expectation. But if you have an unfair advantage that you have an understanding, even a foundational machine learning understanding, it will make you and make whatever you build a lot more rich in terms of not just the features but the ability to deliver more predictable experiences versus many times very unpredictable UI experiences using Gen AI.
Next episode: Time series forecasting and anomaly detection (because not everything is classification and regression).

- Consider transformation (if the dataset is highly skewed, do some stuff to adjust for that - this is more of an advanced topic)
SMOTE explained: When you have a very imbalanced dataset, good examples are again the cancer dataset where 1-5% might have a diagnosis while 90+ don't.
There's different ways that you can amplify the signal of the ones that do have it. SMOTE in plain English is you synthetically increase the number of examples for the imbalance class.
In this case, the number of people that would be diagnosed to really amplify the signal of what the machine learning model should look for.

Because if it's so imbalanced and you're looking to predict this little diamond in the rough and you have one piece of light amongst a bunch of darkness, really hard for math to do its thing and generalize well.
Model selection: I told it go through a baseline linear model (logistic regression, I reviewed that in day one and day two).
Hyperparameter tuning: This is basically of all the parameters and levers that you can adjust in a particular model. Each model has different ones.
If you dig in you'll see that you have different parameters that you can tune (that's what it's called tuning) and adjust to try and get it to focus better or to not over-index on things.
Deep learning warning: In the world of deep learning you have like 20+ parameters that you can change so it's overwhelming to do deep learning.
One of the other reasons why I never recommend and why it's not recommended for anyone to jump into the deep end and use a black box deep learning model to run predictions.

Not only is it not explainable, but if you don't know what you're doing, you don't appreciate the math behind deep learning, it's really hard to understand why you're choosing certain activation functions.
Deep learning is a beast of its own and it's really hard to be decent at it even with Claude Code if you have no clue what you're doing.
Evaluation: How to evaluate the test sets and what metrics it should use.
Feature importance and explanation: Trying to understand which parameters in the dataset are of the most importance.

Packaging: In this case I'm telling it right now to just run it locally so I can play with it. I'll worry about production later. Right now I'm not talking about production, I'm mentioning what we want to do right now.
The Claude Code process:
All we had was the
goal.md
file and the application CSV file.

Once I did this, I then run /init like you've seen me do many times before. This will analyze the code base, it will come up with an understanding, then it reads the goal file, puts everything together, and now it creates this
claude.md
file with an understanding of both files.
I've primed Claude Code to get ready for this. Now I say: Create a plan to execute this in one shot.

It comes up with a plan. It says it's going to create this file called an IPYNB file. If you saw my videos on Google Colab, you have a .py file (that's a Python file). An IPYNB file is a Python file that is in a Jupyter Notebook fashion. So it's a much more visual Python file.
It has markdown, it has explanations as to what's happening in the code itself. Let's say fancy Python file if we want to make it clear cut.
Walking through the different phases:
- Web applications
- Documentation and setup
- Final artifacts (a model file, model metadata, the app itself)
- It's going to create its own API using FastAPI
All of this, again, something that would take days to weeks even with someone that was an intermediate to advanced practitioner. Now you can do this really quickly.
It goes through, creates a to-do list, runs all of this beautiful stuff, goes through, creates inference model, then creates an API to use the model.
The first model disaster:
Let me tell you, the first model it came up with was garbage.
It basically predicted that anyone, no matter how good the credit score, even if they were rocking a million dollars and zero debt and perfect credit score, would get rejected.
I could tell right away that was a flawed model. That's why this is a very iterative process.
It comes up finally with this implementation. Then I tell it: Okay cool, you came up with the implementation, please run it because it tells you here how to use it and how to access it.
I just told it: Well you have access to bash which is the ability to control my computer. I can't see it on
localhost
, it's an easy issue.
Eventually it runs it and it tells me: All you have to do now is train the model on the data.
I'm like okay well you do it. "You train it" - you can see how sassy I am. I tried to do this on purpose to show you how easy it could be without me going fancy on the prompting.

I could go fancy on the prompting. I could spin up a couple sub-agents to run each part of this training process in parallel. I can really flex in terms of my ability to make this faster and easier, but I just wanted to show you how easy you could do it with minimal understanding of ML principles.
The training process:
Now it updates everything, it runs the training script. It's training on a portion of the data, typically 50-60% of the dataset.
Of 10,000 rows of training from the applications I showed you, it will take around 5-6,000.
Now it's training on everything, takes a sweet time, and then eventually it comes back with this model.
It lies to my face initially. It says it's trained and then it notices itself that the performance is kind of suspect.
Once I saw that I'm like this is going to be an awful model.
It says it's complete, the approval system is live, it runs on
localhost
. Then I go and run some predictions and they are absolutely horrific.

Now it says approval probability is 20%, 30%. Eventually I go back and forth and I tell it: Listen, you're predicting everything as negative. Let's retrain the model because it seems like there's some imbalance here.

This is what's happening in between back and forth. You don't have to say there's some imbalance. You just say the results are trash. You could literally say that. You could screenshot: "This is trash. It seems like no matter what I do, people are being predicted as negative or predicted as being rejected."
Diagnosing the problem:
Then I ask it a question: Is the model the best we can do in terms of performance?
Now it goes through, runs the machine learning model on some predictions, it analyzes its own data.
Well well, look at this. It realizes there's a class imbalance in the data: 90% of the 10,000 rows were rejected, only 8% were approved.
Like my cancer example, we have this here. Now it goes through a plan on how to improve this.
The fixes it implemented:

It improved the features: It created brand new fields. It used some of the fields to create new features and now creates a new feature called "financial health" which is kind of like a proxy for a few different fields.

This is what I was referring to in lecture one and two: Sometimes you aren't just constrained by the data you're given to run a machine learning model. You can use those fields to create brand new composite fields that you can use to give the model a better end in terms of its next training steps.
Better hyperparameter tuning: I told you we have parameters for different models. It picked the model and then it was able to play around with the features.

In this case it used XGBoost which I referred to in my last video. When in doubt people use XGBoost. Are there better models? Absolutely, especially now. I saw one the other day that beats XGBoost. But for now we're gonna use that.
Class imbalance handling: It created a balanced weighting for different approvals, it focused more on the minority class.
I mentioned one way you can do this - there's many mathematical ways you can amplify the signal of a smaller class.
Model comparison: This is what it cranked out before. It goes through key findings of improvements in the model. It generates that matrix I showed you last day on false positives and true negatives.
It found out what I said: It basically never predicts approval for anyone before.
Now after going through, you can read through everything it did, it comes up with the new architecture it came up with.
I was able to run its own model which is cool to come up with the bottom line.
Deployment to Modal:
Now I ask the question: What do we have to do to serve this online?

What I used to do is serve it on something like Amazon. You have different ways to serve it on Amazon. One of them is using AWS SageMaker (a bit more expensive, something I wouldn't use as much at least back in the day - it's much cheaper now but not by much).
If you were stuck back in the day and you didn't want to code as much, you would use something like AWS SageMaker or GCP Cloud Run.
It comes up with some examples. The easiest method it recommends is Modal which is the one I'm showing you today.
It is really straightforward once you install everything. It'll show you what the process looks like. Then it'll go through the deployment options.
You'll see the hardest one is the one I used to do which is the AWS, Azure, and GCP. You have different things like Digital Ocean.
Heroku: This one is no longer relevant. Heroku used to be the hero back in the day but nobody, I don't know a single human being that does ML to this day that uses it, but still an option.
Then this is what will happen after deployment. It gives you a full guide. It tells you: Use Modal.
It tells you go and run this, go and install this. As usual I say: Do it yourself please. Can you run all the bash and bring me in when I'm needed?
The Modal installation process:

It tries to do it but it seems like it struggles a bit. One thing I noticed is it was easier for me to use Warp and I just used its commands because Claude was kind of not hallucinating but it said it was installed at the beginning but it wasn't.
I just ran the exact commands you see here: pip install, modal setup, modal deploy.
It finally installs it after I get the right command: python3 -m pip install (if you're on Windows or Linux it might be different for you).
Within five minutes it was able to get it. It told me that I needed to upgrade pip. Pip allows you to install libraries on your computer and other things as well.
Then I can run pip install modal. I follow the instructions. I say modal setup. Then it makes me log in, creating an account.

Once you create an account (again it's free - I think you have $5 for free and if you share something you get $30 for free), it's really cheap to run at scale. You won't use that very quickly. It's not like an LLM.
Then I made my new workspace, I logged in, I had a new token and all this, but it was just me clicking through Modal. Nothing fancy here.
Then I just imported this function that Modal asked me to test out to see whether it works or not. It tells you that authentication is finished successfully. Pretty much I was good from there.
After that point, once I did the bash outside of here in Warp, we were good to go.
Deployment success:
Your app is deployed and live. It gives you the link to what we saw, which was this version.
This is what the app looked like on
localhost
. This is where I went back and forth and I tested it out. I can run this and get prediction. Finally we have some proof.
Then I said okay cool, let's deploy it. Once we deploy it, we go on here on the app itself. We go on overview. You can see, you can click on this.
You can see Claude made an API for us. This API has a method or a section called /predict. Anytime you see 200 OK, meaning it ran perfectly fine.
You can see performance, you can see how it's going. Most of the time this is super straightforward.

What's awesome is if I go back to here you can see all the times I've ran this. All the predictions, you can see every time the status of how it went. This is pretty standard, there's nothing crazy here.
It tells you how quick it is. This should be blazing fast because this is not some Gen AI reasoning model.
Creating the Vercel frontend:
This is all done. This point we were good to go. This is all live and working.
Now it also creates some docs for me, some API docs as well. It created the file.
Now I asked it curious: Would I be able to hit this API from another app on Vercel now?

I know the answer to this is yes but I wanted to show you this: Now that this API exists and it's hosted on a server and we basically create a zip file or compression of this knowledge understanding from the model, you can now hit it from anywhere you want.
Then it tells me how this would be done, it gives me a bunch of code that I don't need to use.
Then I say just this: Let's create an app just like this one but one I can host on Vercel.

It goes and builds the app that I've been showing you up until now. It makes and rebuilds the entire same UI, everything, as well as the predictions. Then it gives me the location of all the core information.
It runs it and then I basically say: Create a brand new GitHub repo.
This is all I'm saying by the way, nothing else happened. This is all Claude just telling me what it did.

It builds a GitHub repo. Now that I had that repo, all I had to do was go back to Vercel, add new project. Now that I had it committed to GitHub, I just had to click mortgage app import and that was pretty much it.
Because it was able to just code the new API documentation of this.
This is the app ID and you can see it can see basically how to run everything. You can see up until now I've only used 3 cents.
It was able to use the exact API and now you can use this from anywhere.
The bigger picture:
You can have an app with technically 10-15 different ML functions if you wanted. I don't recommend it but you could.

You can make really robust apps where maybe 60% is still Gen AI, maybe natural language stuff, maybe knowledge-based RAG stuff, but you can now add components that are a lot richer, a lot more explainable, things that you have a handle over how they'll perform in the wild.
This is one small sliver of what you can do and how you can go from an idea to something that you can push to production.
You could see here my involvement in this process was minimal.
What I'll do is I will make the two files I used available as well as the GitHub repo to you in case it's helpful to you to see how it was built, how it's structured.
You can copy the way I mimicked it. But outside of that you can see that there was minimal intervention from me, prompting it very smart and nerdy things.

This goes from something run on Modal (the platform that hosts machine learning models after training) and then we can actually integrate it in whatever app we want.
That gives us flexibility and it will give you a different edge, especially when you go out in the world and you build vibe-coded apps.

Natural language stuff is now gonna be the expectation. lessons.title: 4) Running Multiple Machine Learning Algorithms
lessons.description:
in Parallel for Enhanced Predictions
ML Mini Series Day 4: Run AI Predictions at HYPERSCALE 🔋🔌
Machine learning super leverage.
What if you could run 40+ models at once? And have Claude Code do it for you...
Well... you can (even if you don't understand a line of code)
25 minutes showing you how to stop guessing which ML algorithm to use - run ALL of them simultaneously, let math pick the winner, then optimize it automatically.
What you'll watch:
- Why running one algorithm at a time is amateur hour
- LazyPredict: screen 40+ models in under 5 minutes
- Auto-sklearn: optimize the winner's parameters automatically
- PyCaret walkthrough (the OG library from my master's days)
- Building a full Streamlit dashboard with interactive predictions
- Business insights that would take me weeks to compile manually
- A live churn predictor you can play with
The gentleman on the left vs the bad boy on the right:
You don't want to be the person manually running one algorithm at a time, tweaking parameters, waiting, running another one, tweaking more parameters, waiting again.
Our goal is to click one button (or run one block of code) and have 40+ algorithms run in parallel, then have the results ranked for us automatically.
These algorithms I'm talking about—if you're not familiar—include things like:
- LightGBM
- Artificial neural networks
- Linear regression
- Logistic regression (both of those we've seen)
- Decision trees
- Random forest
- SVM (support vector machine—very slow, don't use as much anymore, but once in a while it performs better on a particular dataset)
- XGBoost
- And dozens more
We don't want to handle all this manually. So we use libraries that do the heavy lifting.
The three libraries I reference:
Library #1 - PyCaret (the OG):
This is a library that someone from my master's program put together. They still update it to this day.
The way it works: It helps you with data preprocessing to set everything up. It can help you with missing values. It can help you with the imbalance of the dataset. And then it runs all of the algorithms for you.
If I could summarize everything in this video, it would be this one screenshot: PyCaret running all these different ML algorithms at once, and by the end it auto-highlights which ones are the best performing.
Now you don't need this kind of highlighting anymore because Claude Code will do that for you. We didn't have something as smart as Claude Code back then—we needed a smart library with smart results.
So you can then see: Okay, logistic regression seems best at accuracy. Linear discriminant analysis (which I don't even know what this one is—I can remember very vaguely, but that's the whole point) is performing at 0.8 AUC. And this one's performing best on recall.
That's why this makes your life a lot easier. You can analyze results, find feature importance, understand which elements of the data are most relevant to each model.
Library #2 - LazyPredict (what I use today):
LazyPredict does very similar to what you just saw, just does it a lot faster. It's also been updated as of a few months ago.
Library #3 - Auto-sklearn:
Sklearn (if you don't know what that word is) is a very popular library for machine learning algorithms. It's the one I used back in the day. Still used today because it has pretty much all the different algorithms you could use.
Auto-sklearn allows you to take the best model (or models) from LazyPredict and optimize what parameters and what values those parameters should have.
The two-stage workflow:
Stage 1: Rapid Model Screening with LazyPredict
- Quickly evaluate 40 machine learning models
- Identify promising algorithm families for churn prediction
- Compare all the main metrics
- Decide on top 3-5 model candidates
Stage 2: Optimization with Auto-sklearn
- Perform robust Bayesian optimization on the promising models identified in Stage 1
- This is AI lingo for: optimize the parameters of that model
- Find the best max_depth, learning rate, regularization values automatically
You can use whatever combination you want. You could just use LazyPredict. I'm showing you both.
The setup (how I fed Claude Code):
I only started with one file. And this file—I am no genius—I had AI come up with it.
I told it: I want to use LazyPredict and I want to use Auto-sklearn. First I want LazyPredict to run all the algorithms in parallel and pick the best ones. Then whatever ones are the best, I want Auto-sklearn to find and optimize the best parameters.
This file is an overview for Claude walking through the workflow strategy:
Workflow Strategy Stage 1:
- Run rapid model screening with LazyPredict
- Quickly evaluate 40 machine learning models
- Identify promising algorithm families for churn prediction
Stage 2:
- Optimization with Auto-sklearn
- Performing robust Bayesian optimization on the promising model
- Basically just saying: optimize the parameters of that model
The file includes examples of how to use Auto-sklearn and how to use LazyPredict. I basically gave all the documentation to Claude AI on the browser and said: Go make a prompt optimized for Claude Code. Go do research on Claude Code. Go do research on the latest version of LazyPredict and Auto-sklearn and help give as many hints as possible for Claude Code as of November 2025.
Even if you have no clue what code looks like, you'd see the main function called lazy classifier. This is where everything else comes in and runs its prediction.
The file goes through best practices for churn prediction—look out for whether or not the classes are imbalanced in a dataset. It then gives an overview of the dataset. I fed it the dataset on Claude.ai on the front end to basically tailor the instructions to that specific dataset.
Then it adds reference documentation in case Claude Code wants to do research on those URLs itself.
The dataset (customer churn prediction):
The dataset I'm using is for churn prediction—deciding or trying to predict when a certain customer will leave your service or your company.
This is great for business context because if you can predict which users are most likely to leave, then you can:
- Send them personalized offers
- Try to upsell them ahead of time
- Offer them an annual subscription at 50% off
- All kinds of business implications
10,000 rows with the following columns:
- Customer age
- Account age (how long their account has been active)
- Monthly charges
- Lifetime value charges
- Contract type (month-to-month vs annual vs two-year)
- Payment method
- Internet service
- Support tickets (how many they've sent)
- Satisfaction score
- Number of services they have with the provider
- Tech support
- Online backup
- Paperless billing
- Average monthly usage in gigabytes
Support tickets sidebar: I would imagine this is important because if someone sends nothing or sends way too many, you would imagine either they're super frustrated and not getting issues resolved, or they're just dead silent.
The target variable: Anyone that has a 1 is a customer that churned.
The Claude Code process:
Once I had both the dataset and the context file, all I did was /init. It does its thing. It comes back saying: Alright, I see both of those files. I'll create a claude.md file with an understanding of both files and that we're trying to do the two-stage LazyPredict to Auto-sklearn workflow.
Then it says: I need you to implement a complete AutoML workflow for customer churn prediction using the provided dataset and context documentation. Please execute the following...
I give it an overview of the tasks. I had AI create this prompt just to reinforce whatever is in the claude.md. Nothing too crazy—just me saying perform a train and test split where 80% is meant for training.
It analyzes, reads the whole file, creates a plan. It's going to create an IPYNB file (a Jupyter Notebook—a special Python file specifically made for running ML algorithms really quickly).
The five-part plan:
Part 1: Data prep and exploration
Part 2: LazyPredict screening (looks for top 10 models, identifies top 3 of those)
Part 3: Auto-sklearn optimization
Part 4: Model comparison
Part 5: Business insights
What happens in machine learning is you do all this work, come up with results, and most of them are numerical or statistical. So you (or you used to) as a data scientist have to spend the next week trying to understand the results and put words to them.
Lucky for you, Claude can do this for you.
The execution:
It builds one part at a time. Pro tip: You can add a hashtag like "as you finish each part, stop and tell me where you're at." Then between each part, you can do /clear to get your context window back.
You might also want to create the to-do list as a .md file so you can use it as a checklist for preservation of the context window.
In this case, it took around 15-20 minutes to run all of them.
Then, like before, it gives me all the files but it didn't actually run the ML algorithm yet.
So as usual, I'm nice and sassy: "You run it and do all the training."
Now it runs everything it set up. One thing you might want to add to instructions: Don't just come up with the artifacts and assets—actually run the ML algorithms.
Everything installs. It finally comes back with: Workflow completed successfully.
The results (this is where it gets beautiful):
It gives you a table that looks kind of mismatched. Key insights include:
- Contract type: Month-to-month contracts have 90% churn versus 42% for two-year contracts (big surprise, right?)
- Satisfaction score correlation: -0.25 with churn (lower satisfaction equals higher churn)
None of this is groundbreaking. But it shows there's an understanding of the data without it being a language model. This isn't ChatGPT doing this. Math is able to find this, which is helpful because math scales.
You can't just give 10 billion rows to Gemini 2.0 because you have a million-token context window. If you have a billion rows, what are you gonna do? Iterate on it over and over 100 times? You could, but you'll have hallucination. At least you have math at your side here.
The Streamlit dashboard:
I said: Create a dashboard on localhost walking me through all the results and make it interactive and intuitive. Feel free to embed your own plots.
It created a bunch of visualizations without me asking. But I wanted this on a dashboard.
It realized it should use Streamlit. Streamlit is a very lightweight visualization tool through Python to show results and build reports. Streamlit was the OG vibe coding—before Netlify, before quick React apps, you could spin up a Streamlit reasonably quickly.
The dashboard breakdown:
Section 1 - Overview:
- 10,000 customers
- 71% churned (this company is toast)
- Which model performed best
- How many models were evaluated
Section 2 - Data Exploration:
- Snippet of the data (in Python this would be done with df.head(10)—you don't have to do that because Claude Code does it for you)
- Feature statistics: average customer age, average account age
- All the things you do during the EDA (exploration) process
Section 3 - Interactive Visualizations:
- Contract by type distribution
- Customer distribution by contract type
- Key insights for model selection
Section 4 - Model Selection:
- Best performing model: XGBoost (surprise surprise)
- Model families it went through
- Why XGBoost with limited depth won
Max depth explained: One of the parameters of XGBoost is max_depth—basically how deep should this tree go? The deeper it goes, the higher the likelihood that the algorithm memorizes the dataset versus understands the underlying patterns. It decided through testing that limited depth was the best result.
Other parameters shown: Learning rate, regularization
Section 5 - The Model Funnel (super cool):
A visual funnel showing:
- All classifiers assessed (40+)
- Top 10 performers
- Tree-based models (XGBoost, LightGBM, etc.)
- Final optimized model
It even walks through why we used LazyPredict if you wanted to explain it to a client or your team.
Section 6 - Model Performance:
All the models it ran and how they performed overall. The exact same thing I showed you in PyCaret—you get it here. All the results for all the algorithms.
This is why this is so high leverage. Especially if you don't know what you're doing, you can look like you know what you're doing.
I'm joking, but you can run a series of hypothetical realities before you break your neck trying to understand each algorithm.
Tangible example: Let's say you don't care to learn what Linear Discriminant Analysis is. When you look at the results, it's near the bottom. You know what? It might not be worth understanding because it clearly sucks on this dataset.
Whereas XGBoost, Extra Trees, anything tree-related like Random Forest—those are crushing it. Good instinct: You should probably know what these are. Do some research, watch a couple YouTube videos, familiarize yourself with how they work.
Section 7 - Confusion Matrix and Curves:
- True positives vs true negatives
- False positives vs false negatives
- ROC curves
If you don't know how to read these curves, upload them to Claude literally and say: Walk me through step by step like I'm in grade 10 what this is doing.
Section 8 - Business Insights (the churn insights):
This is why this is so cool. Top 10 features driving customer churn:
1. Contract type
2. Account age by months
3. Satisfaction score
4. Support tickets
5. Payment method
6. Number of services
7. Total charges
8. Tech support
Contract type insights:
- Low satisfaction score: 93% churn
- High satisfaction score: 39% churn
Look at the y-axis. This is telling you things are bad. The service is horrific.
Support tickets insights:
- More support tickets = things suck
- But zero support tickets also has quite a bit of churn
- 10+ support tickets? You are cooked. Absolutely cooked.
Account tenure insights:
- 0-6 months: 83% churn (horrific)
- 6-12 months: 78%
- 12-24 months: 72%
- 2-3+ years: Lower churn (they've settled with this horrific service)
Section 9 - Recommendations:
It comes up with recommended actions by segment:
High risk (60%+):
- Personal call from the retention team
- Exclusive loyalty discount
- Free upgrade to premium tier for three months
- Dedicated account manager
Medium risk:
- Automated email sequences
- Satisfaction surveys
Low risk:
- Standard engagement
This is awesome. You can run all the ML algorithms, have Claude Code sprinkle in some GenAI where it makes sense to interpret them, and come up with business recommendations.
You could look like an absolute rock star if you bring the skill set we're trying to upskill you with—the generative AI side married with the ML data analysis side.
Section 10 - The Live Churn Predictor:
I asked it to create a section where you can actually run the model.
Input fields:
- Customer age
- Contract type
- Account age months
- And more
Example prediction:
- 45-year-old on a two-year contract, account age 17 months
- Click predict (see how quick that is)
- Result: 25% churn probability
Now change to month-to-month:
- Result: 90% churn probability
That's what's so beautiful about this. It's free. I'm not incurring API cost every time this runs. The model has already learned. Now that it's learned, we're just hitting its set of weights or predictions with this interpretation of different metrics.
This would make a great presentation.
The Google Colab sidebar (brand new):
If you go to extensions, you can now connect Google Colab to Cursor or VS Code.
Think about it: You can use an actual Google Colab notebook in the cloud that you sync to Claude Code, and you can rent the free GPU they give you on Colab.
If you have a very large dataset, theoretically (this is like a couple weeks old) you can rent a TPU or GPU to run the algorithms—especially if you have very large data and comprehensive algorithms—and still port the code back to Claude Code for interpretation, visualization, etc.
You have a lot of options.
The goal of this series:
Run ML algorithms at scale AND understand the business application.
It's one thing to run analysis. It's another layer to be able to contextualize that analysis, to make it understandable and actionable.
Before: Spend weeks setting up the web page, setting up the analytics, building Excel reports, creating PowerPoint decks.
Now: Do it using something like Streamlit very quickly with Claude Code.
This is how you become dangerous.

- SVM (support vector machine—very slow, don't use as much anymore, but once in a while it performs better on a particular dataset)
- XGBoost
- And dozens more
We don't want to handle all this manually. So we use libraries that do the heavy lifting.
The three libraries I reference:
Library #1 - PyCaret (the OG):
This is a library that someone from my master's program put together. They still update it to this day.

The way it works: It helps you with data preprocessing to set everything up. It can help you with missing values. It can help you with the imbalance of the dataset. And then it runs all of the algorithms for you.

If I could summarize everything in this video, it would be this one screenshot: PyCaret running all these different ML algorithms at once, and by the end it auto-highlights which ones are the best performing.
Now you don't need this kind of highlighting anymore because Claude Code will do that for you. We didn't have something as smart as Claude Code back then—we needed a smart library with smart results.

So you can then see: Okay, logistic regression seems best at accuracy. Linear discriminant analysis (which I don't even know what this one is—I can remember very vaguely, but that's the whole point) is performing at 0.8 AUC. And this one's performing best on recall.
That's why this makes your life a lot easier. You can analyze results, find feature importance, understand which elements of the data are most relevant to each model.
Library #2 - LazyPredict (what I use today):
LazyPredict does very similar to what you just saw, just does it a lot faster. It's also been updated as of a few months ago.
Library #3 - Auto-sklearn:

Sklearn (if you don't know what that word is) is a very popular library for machine learning algorithms. It's the one I used back in the day. Still used today because it has pretty much all the different algorithms you could use.
Auto-sklearn allows you to take the best model (or models) from LazyPredict and optimize what parameters and what values those parameters should have.
The two-stage workflow:
Stage 1: Rapid Model Screening with LazyPredict
- Quickly evaluate 40 machine learning models
- Identify promising algorithm families for churn prediction
- Compare all the main metrics
- Decide on top 3-5 model candidates
Stage 2: Optimization with Auto-sklearn
- Perform robust Bayesian optimization on the promising models identified in Stage 1
- This is AI lingo for: optimize the parameters of that model
- Find the best max_depth, learning rate, regularization values automatically
You can use whatever combination you want. You could just use LazyPredict. I'm showing you both.
The setup (how I fed Claude Code):
I only started with one file. And this file—I am no genius—I had AI come up with it.

I told it: I want to use LazyPredict and I want to use Auto-sklearn. First I want LazyPredict to run all the algorithms in parallel and pick the best ones. Then whatever ones are the best, I want Auto-sklearn to find and optimize the best parameters.
This file is an overview for Claude walking through the workflow strategy:
Workflow Strategy Stage 1:
- Run rapid model screening with LazyPredict
- Quickly evaluate 40 machine learning models
- Identify promising algorithm families for churn prediction
Stage 2:
- Optimization with Auto-sklearn
- Performing robust Bayesian optimization on the promising model
- Basically just saying: optimize the parameters of that model

The file includes examples of how to use Auto-sklearn and how to use LazyPredict. I basically gave all the documentation to Claude AI on the browser and said: Go make a prompt optimized for Claude Code. Go do research on Claude Code. Go do research on the latest version of LazyPredict and Auto-sklearn and help give as many hints as possible for Claude Code as of November 2025.
Even if you have no clue what code looks like, you'd see the main function called lazy classifier. This is where everything else comes in and runs its prediction.
The file goes through best practices for churn prediction—look out for whether or not the classes are imbalanced in a dataset. It then gives an overview of the dataset. I fed it the dataset on
Claude.ai
on the front end to basically tailor the instructions to that specific dataset.
Then it adds reference documentation in case Claude Code wants to do research on those URLs itself.
The dataset (customer churn prediction):
The dataset I'm using is for churn prediction—deciding or trying to predict when a certain customer will leave your service or your company.
This is great for business context because if you can predict which users are most likely to leave, then you can:
- Send them personalized offers
- Try to upsell them ahead of time
- Offer them an annual subscription at 50% off
- All kinds of business implications
10,000 rows with the following columns:
- Customer age
- Account age (how long their account has been active)
- Monthly charges
- Lifetime value charges
- Contract type (month-to-month vs annual vs two-year)
- Payment method
- Internet service
- Support tickets (how many they've sent)
- Satisfaction score
- Number of services they have with the provider
- Tech support
- Online backup
- Paperless billing
- Average monthly usage in gigabytes

Support tickets sidebar: I would imagine this is important because if someone sends nothing or sends way too many, you would imagine either they're super frustrated and not getting issues resolved, or they're just dead silent.
The target variable: Anyone that has a 1 is a customer that churned.
The Claude Code process:
Once I had both the dataset and the context file, all I did was /init. It does its thing. It comes back saying: Alright, I see both of those files. I'll create a
claude.md
file with an understanding of both files and that we're trying to do the two-stage LazyPredict to Auto-sklearn workflow.
Then it says: I need you to implement a complete AutoML workflow for customer churn prediction using the provided dataset and context documentation. Please execute the following...
I give it an overview of the tasks. I had AI create this prompt just to reinforce whatever is in the
claude.md
. Nothing too crazy—just me saying perform a train and test split where 80% is meant for training.
It analyzes, reads the whole file, creates a plan. It's going to create an IPYNB file (a Jupyter Notebook—a special Python file specifically made for running ML algorithms really quickly).
The five-part plan:
Part 1: Data prep and exploration
Part 2: LazyPredict screening (looks for top 10 models, identifies top 3 of those)
Part 3: Auto-sklearn optimization
Part 4: Model comparison
Part 5: Business insights

What happens in machine learning is you do all this work, come up with results, and most of them are numerical or statistical. So you (or you used to) as a data scientist have to spend the next week trying to understand the results and put words to them.
Lucky for you, Claude can do this for you.
The execution:

It builds one part at a time. Pro tip: You can add a hashtag like "as you finish each part, stop and tell me where you're at." Then between each part, you can do /clear to get your context window back.
You might also want to create the to-do list as a .md file so you can use it as a checklist for preservation of the context window.
In this case, it took around 15-20 minutes to run all of them.
Then, like before, it gives me all the files but it didn't actually run the ML algorithm yet.
So as usual, I'm nice and sassy: "You run it and do all the training."
Now it runs everything it set up. One thing you might want to add to instructions: Don't just come up with the artifacts and assets—actually run the ML algorithms.
Everything installs. It finally comes back with: Workflow completed successfully.
The results (this is where it gets beautiful):
It gives you a table that looks kind of mismatched. Key insights include:
- Contract type: Month-to-month contracts have 90% churn versus 42% for two-year contracts (big surprise, right?)
- Satisfaction score correlation: -0.25 with churn (lower satisfaction equals higher churn)

None of this is groundbreaking. But it shows there's an understanding of the data without it being a language model. This isn't ChatGPT doing this. Math is able to find this, which is helpful because math scales.

You can't just give 10 billion rows to Gemini 2.0 because you have a million-token context window. If you have a billion rows, what are you gonna do? Iterate on it over and over 100 times? You could, but you'll have hallucination. At least you have math at your side here.
The Streamlit dashboard:
I said: Create a dashboard on
localhost
walking me through all the results and make it interactive and intuitive. Feel free to embed your own plots.
It created a bunch of visualizations without me asking. But I wanted this on a dashboard.

It realized it should use Streamlit. Streamlit is a very lightweight visualization tool through Python to show results and build reports. Streamlit was the OG vibe coding—before Netlify, before quick React apps, you could spin up a Streamlit reasonably quickly.
The dashboard breakdown:
Section 1 - Overview:
- 10,000 customers
- 71% churned (this company is toast)
- Which model performed best
- How many models were evaluated
Section 2 - Data Exploration:
- Snippet of the data (in Python this would be done with df.head(10)—you don't have to do that because Claude Code does it for you)
- Feature statistics: average customer age, average account age
- All the things you do during the EDA (exploration) process
Section 3 - Interactive Visualizations:
- Contract by type distribution
- Customer distribution by contract type
- Key insights for model selection
Section 4 - Model Selection:
- Best performing model: XGBoost (surprise surprise)
- Model families it went through
- Why XGBoost with limited depth won

Max depth explained: One of the parameters of XGBoost is max_depth—basically how deep should this tree go? The deeper it goes, the higher the likelihood that the algorithm memorizes the dataset versus understands the underlying patterns. It decided through testing that limited depth was the best result.
Other parameters shown: Learning rate, regularization
Section 5 - The Model Funnel (super cool):
A visual funnel showing:
- All classifiers assessed (40+)
- Top 10 performers
- Tree-based models (XGBoost, LightGBM, etc.)
- Final optimized model
It even walks through why we used LazyPredict if you wanted to explain it to a client or your team.
Section 6 - Model Performance:
All the models it ran and how they performed overall. The exact same thing I showed you in PyCaret—you get it here. All the results for all the algorithms.
This is why this is so high leverage. Especially if you don't know what you're doing, you can look like you know what you're doing.
I'm joking, but you can run a series of hypothetical realities before you break your neck trying to understand each algorithm.

Tangible example: Let's say you don't care to learn what Linear Discriminant Analysis is. When you look at the results, it's near the bottom. You know what? It might not be worth understanding because it clearly sucks on this dataset.

Whereas XGBoost, Extra Trees, anything tree-related like Random Forest—those are crushing it. Good instinct: You should probably know what these are. Do some research, watch a couple YouTube videos, familiarize yourself with how they work.
Section 7 - Confusion Matrix and Curves:
- True positives vs true negatives
- False positives vs false negatives
- ROC curves
If you don't know how to read these curves, upload them to Claude literally and say: Walk me through step by step like I'm in grade 10 what this is doing.
Section 8 - Business Insights (the churn insights):
This is why this is so cool. Top 10 features driving customer churn:
1. Contract type
2. Account age by months
3. Satisfaction score
4. Support tickets
5. Payment method
6. Number of services
7. Total charges
8. Tech support
Contract type insights:
- Low satisfaction score: 93% churn
- High satisfaction score: 39% churn
Look at the y-axis. This is telling you things are bad. The service is horrific.
Support tickets insights:
- More support tickets = things suck
- But zero support tickets also has quite a bit of churn
- 10+ support tickets? You are cooked. Absolutely cooked.
Account tenure insights:
- 0-6 months: 83% churn (horrific)
- 6-12 months: 78%
- 2-3+ years: Lower churn (they've settled with this horrific service)
Section 9 - Recommendations:
It comes up with recommended actions by segment:
High risk (60%+):
- Personal call from the retention team
- Exclusive loyalty discount
- Free upgrade to premium tier for three months
- Dedicated account manager
Medium risk:
- Automated email sequences
- Satisfaction surveys
Low risk:
- Standard engagement
This is awesome. You can run all the ML algorithms, have Claude Code sprinkle in some GenAI where it makes sense to interpret them, and come up with business recommendations.
You could look like an absolute rock star if you bring the skill set we're trying to upskill you with—the generative AI side married with the ML data analysis side.
Section 10 - The Live Churn Predictor:
I asked it to create a section where you can actually run the model.
Input fields:
- Customer age
- Contract type
- Account age months
- And more
Example prediction:
- 45-year-old on a two-year contract, account age 17 months
- Click predict (see how quick that is)
- Result: 25% churn probability
Now change to month-to-month:
- Result: 90% churn probability

That's what's so beautiful about this. It's free. I'm not incurring API cost every time this runs. The model has already learned. Now that it's learned, we're just hitting its set of weights or predictions with this interpretation of different metrics.
This would make a great presentation.
The Google Colab sidebar (brand new):
If you go to extensions, you can now connect Google Colab to Cursor or VS Code.
Think about it: You can use an actual Google Colab notebook in the cloud that you sync to Claude Code, and you can rent the free GPU they give you on Colab.

If you have a very large dataset, theoretically (this is like a couple weeks old) you can rent a TPU or GPU to run the algorithms—especially if you have very large data and comprehensive algorithms—and still port the code back to Claude Code for interpretation, visualization, etc.
You have a lot of options.
The goal of this series:
Run ML algorithms at scale AND understand the business application.
It's one thing to run analysis. It's another layer to be able to contextualize that analysis, to make it understandable and actionable.
Before: Spend weeks setting up the web page, setting up the analytics, building Excel reports, creating PowerPoint decks.
Now: Do it using something like Streamlit very quickly with Claude Code.
This is how you become dangerous.

lessons.title: Enhancing AI Agent Workflows with Sub-Agents 🤖
lessons.description:
n8n's New Agent-as-Tool Feature --> Build Manager + Employee Agents
🧠 Agent-as-Tool Architecture: You can now add sub-agents as tools directly within a master AI agent node, enabling more modular and scalable agent workflows without chaining outputs manually.
🧰 Tool Stacking & Swarming: Sub-agents can serve distinct roles (e.g., researcher, copy reviewer) under a master agent, enabling hierarchical execution while optionally sharing memory or model resources.
⚙️ Smart Use Cases & Routing: Example implementation uses a router with regex-based intent detection (e.g., billing, bug, demo) to delegate tasks to corresponding specialized master agents and their sub-agents.
💸 Cost-Efficiency Advice: Sub-agents should use cheaper, lower-compute models like GPT-4 mini, while master agents can use higher-end models like Claude or GPT-4.1 Sonnet, based on task complexity.
🚨 Use Thoughtfully: While flexible, adding too many agents can increase hallucination risk and complexity. Use sub-agents when workflows grow too large, context windows overflow, or role separation adds clarity.

lessons.title: 🆕 Simple RAG Setup
lessons.description:
Data Ingestion & Vectorization Flow
Trigger on file upload: Accepts documents via n8n upload interface or webhook from custom front-ends.
Binary data processing: Detects MIME type and extracts raw text automatically.
Recursive text splitting: Breaks documents into optimal chunk sizes for embedding.
OpenAI embedding generation: Converts chunks to vectors using embedding-small model.
Pinecone vector storage: Uploads vectorized chunks to designated index with metadata.Intelligent Retrieval & Response Flow
Chat interface trigger: Listens for queries via n8n chat, webhook, WhatsApp, or Telegram.
Query vectorization: Converts question into matching embedding format.
Semantic search: Queries Pinecone for most relevant chunks based on similarity scoring.
Context-aware AI response: Feeds retrieved chunks + query to GPT-4 with 10-message memory window.
Response delivery: Returns answer through original communication channel.Business Case / Use Case
Solution: Transform static documents into an intelligent, conversational knowledge base—query internal documentation through natural language without manual searching.
Value Proposition
Instant Knowledge Access: Get accurate answers in seconds versus hours of manual file searching.
Reduced Support Burden: Deflect repetitive questions to AI, cutting support costs 40-60%.
Always-Current Responses: Auto-indexes updated documents without retraining models.
Scalable Foundation: Extends easily with tools, multi-modal inputs, or advanced reasoning.Ideal Buyers / Industries
Customer Support Teams: 24/7 self-service for extensive help docs and FAQs.
Professional Services: Quick reference for massive case files, legal precedents, client documents.
Healthcare Organizations: HIPAA-compliant access to protocols, research, patient education.
Internal IT & HR: Automate employee questions on policies, benefits, onboarding, tech docs.
Educational Institutions: Instant student access to course materials, syllabi, research papers.
SaaS Product Teams: In-app AI assistants for product documentation and API references.
Manufacturing & Operations: Rapid access to equipment manuals, safety procedures, compliance docs.

lessons.title: 🆕 Hybrid Context RAG Assistant
lessons.description:
Data Ingestion & Vectorization Flow
Google Drive monitoring: Watches folder for new documents and extracts text content automatically.
OpenAI embedding generation: Converts document chunks to vectors using text-embedding-large model.
Supabase vector storage: Uploads embedded chunks with row indexing for sequential retrieval.Hybrid Retrieval & Response Flow
Chat interface trigger: Receives queries via n8n native chat (configurable for webhook/messaging apps).
Semantic search execution: Agent invokes vector content tool (sub-workflow) to query Supabase for relevant chunks.
Context expansion: JavaScript extracts 2 rows before and 2 after each retrieved chunk for surrounding context.
Context aggregation: Combines semantically relevant chunks + neighboring text into unified context block.
Gemini chat processing: Feeds expanded context to Gemini model (chosen for large context window).
Fallback model: Automatically switches to backup model if primary times out or hits token limits.Business Case / Use Case
Solution: A RAG system that retrieves not just semantically relevant chunks, but also surrounding context—delivering more accurate answers for complex queries where nuance and sequential information matter.
Value Proposition
Higher Answer Accuracy: Contextual "before and after" chunks reduce misinterpretation from isolated text fragments.
Better Narrative Understanding: Maintains document flow and relationships between concepts that pure semantic search misses.
Intelligent Fallback: Auto-switches models to prevent workflow failures from oversized context windows.
Flexible Context Control: Adjust retrieval depth (rows before/after) based on accuracy vs. cost tradeoffs.Ideal Buyers / Industries
Legal & Compliance Teams: Contracts, policies, and regulations where surrounding clauses are critical to interpretation.
Technical Documentation: API docs, system manuals where step sequences and prerequisites matter.
Medical Research: Clinical studies and treatment protocols requiring full context around findings and contraindications.
Financial Services: Loan agreements, investment prospectuses where terms reference other sections.
Academic Research: Scholarly papers where arguments build on previous paragraphs and citations.
Customer Support (Complex Products): Troubleshooting guides where multi-step processes require sequential context.

lessons.title: 🆕 Re-Ranking RAG Assistant
lessons.description:
Data Ingestion & Vectorization Flow
Google Drive monitoring: Watches folder for new documents and extracts text content automatically.
OpenAI embedding generation: Converts document chunks to vectors using specified embedding model.
Supabase vector storage: Uploads embedded chunks with matching dimension configuration.Re-Ranked Retrieval & Response Flow
Chat interface trigger: Receives queries via n8n native chat (configurable for webhook/messaging apps).
Initial semantic search: Pulls top N chunks (e.g., 20) from Supabase based on embedding similarity.
Cohere re-ranking: Processes retrieved chunks through Cohere re-ranker to score true relevance to query.
Top result filtering: Returns only highest-ranked subset (e.g., top 10) to reduce noise and improve precision.
AI agent response: Feeds re-ranked context to chat model with 20-message memory window.
Consistent embedding models: Uses identical embedding across ingestion and retrieval for accuracy.Business Case / Use Case
Solution: A precision-focused RAG system that performs two-stage retrieval—first semantic search, then intelligent re-ranking—to eliminate marginally relevant results and deliver only the most accurate context.
Value Proposition
Higher Precision Answers: Re-ranking filters semantic search noise, returning truly relevant chunks versus loosely related ones.
Cost Efficiency: Processes fewer tokens by eliminating low-quality context, reducing API costs 30-50%.
Faster Response Times: Smaller, higher-quality context windows mean quicker processing and lower latency.
Better Signal-to-Noise: Eliminates false positives from keyword overlap in large knowledge bases.Ideal Buyers / Industries
Enterprise Knowledge Management: Large organizations with 10,000+ documents where semantic search returns too many marginal matches.
Technical Support Teams: Product documentation with similar terminology across features requiring precise differentiation.
Legal & Compliance: Contract databases where keyword overlap creates false positives but context precision is critical.
Healthcare Information Systems: Medical databases where similar symptoms/treatments need accurate disambiguation.
E-Commerce Platforms: Product catalogs with overlapping descriptions requiring precise matching to user queries.
Academic Research Databases: University libraries needing precise paper recommendations from massive archives.

lessons.title: 🆕 Graph RAG Assistant
lessons.description:
Data Ingestion & Vectorization Flow
Schema-aware data input: Agent receives test data plus table definitions (documents, FAQs, procedures) with relationship mappings.
LLM data classification: Reviews incoming data against schemas to determine correct table assignment.
JSON parsing & validation: Extracts structured data and validates against predefined schema rules.
OpenAI embedding generation: Converts title + content into vectors via HTTP request.
Intelligent routing: Directs data to appropriate Supabase table based on classification (documents/FAQs/procedures).
Relationship preservation: Stores foreign key IDs (related_faq_id, related_procedure_id) in metadata for graph traversal.Graph Retrieval & Response Flow
Multi-table semantic search: Agent queries three separate vector stores (one per data type) simultaneously.
Initial vector retrieval: Returns relevant chunks with embedded relationship IDs in metadata.
Relationship traversal: Uses returned IDs to fetch directly connected records from related tables.
Dual search strategy: Combines semantic search for primary results + direct ID queries for linked context.
Context aggregation: Merges semantically relevant data with relationally connected information for comprehensive answers.Business Case / Use Case
Solution: A graph-based RAG system that understands relationships between different data types—delivering answers that combine semantically relevant content with directly related information across interconnected tables.
Value Proposition
Contextual Completeness: Automatically includes related documents, FAQs, and procedures versus isolated chunks.
Structured Knowledge Navigation: Follows explicit relationships between data types like a human would connect information.
Reduced Hallucination: Leverages defined relationships instead of inferring connections, improving accuracy.
Scalable Data Architecture: Handles complex, multi-entity knowledge bases that simple vector search can't navigate.Ideal Buyers / Industries
Enterprise IT & Support: Documentation systems where guides, troubleshooting steps, and FAQs reference each other.
Healthcare Systems: Medical records linking diagnoses, treatment protocols, medications, and patient histories.
Compliance & Regulatory: Audit systems connecting policies, procedures, incidents, and corrective actions.
Product Development: Engineering docs relating specifications, test procedures, issues, and design decisions.
Legal Services: Case management linking contracts, precedents, filings, and related correspondence.
Educational Platforms: Course materials connecting lectures, assignments, prerequisites, and resources.

lessons.title: Cross-Platform Social Media Publisher
lessons.description:
Solution Breakdown:
Cross-Platform Content Generator
Trigger on Slack messages: Listens to a specific Slack channel for any new message and downloads its text.
Extract “Content Idea”: Parses the message text into a structured “Idea” field for later use.
Save idea to database: Posts the extracted idea as a new record in the “Idea” table (Teable).
AI-driven detail extraction: Feeds the idea through GPT-4 to pull out key points in listicle format.
Multi-format content creation:
LinkedIn/Facebook post: Generates a concise, value-focused post following strict brand guidelines.
Tweets: Crafts standalone tweets (one per key point), ready for X/Twitter.
Instagram carousel: Breaks the idea into 5–20 image-carousel slides (hooks, tips, closing points).
Staging for review: Writes each piece of content back to the “Content” table with status “Review” and platform tags, without immediately publishing.Cross-Platform Content Publisher
Scheduled polling: Every minute (configurable), queries the “Content” table for records where “Status = Approved” and “Scheduled Time ≤ now.”
Record splitting: Separates parent posts from any child (thread) posts.
Aggregate children: If children exist, gathers all replies into a single batch alongside the parent.
AI Agent orchestration: Uses an AI-agent node to:
Post to LinkedIn & Facebook via their respective APIs.
Post parent tweet/thread to X/Twitter (handling threads by chaining child posts).
Status update: After successful posting on each platform, patches the original record to “Published.”
---
Business Case / Use Case
Solution: A turnkey “idea-to-post” system that ingests raw brainstorming (Slack voice notes or text), automatically generates polished multi-platform content, schedules it, and publishes at scale—requiring minimal human intervention beyond initial review.
Value Proposition
Scalability & Efficiency: Eliminates manual copy-writing and posting workflows—marketing teams can do in minutes what once took hours.
Consistency & Governance: Ensures every piece of content adheres to brand voice and compliance guidelines, reducing error risk.
Speed to Market: Rapid turnaround from idea to published post, critical for timely thought-leadership or reactive campaigns.Ideal Buyers / Industries
Digital Marketing Agencies: Manage multiple client accounts across LinkedIn, Facebook, Twitter, Instagram—this automates both creation and scheduling.
Professional Services & Consulting Firms: Thought leaders who need consistent, high-quality social presence without hiring large content teams.
SaaS & Tech Companies: With frequent product updates, blogs, and announcements—automate outreach and engagement.
E-Commerce & Retail Brands: Promote new collections or flash sales across channels with minimal manual effort.
Media & Publishing Houses: Syndicate editorial content intelligently across platforms to maximize reach.
Internal Communications Teams: Automate employee-facing announcements (e.g., HR, operations) via Slack-driven drafts and auto-publishing to intranet channels.

Solution Breakdown:
Automation Summary:
Email Ingestion: Watches an IMAP inbox for new messages and triggers on each incoming email.
Urgency Classification: Uses a GPT-4-powered agent to rate each email’s urgency on a 1–5 scale (4–5 = needs human intervention).

If no input, automatically sends a “team is busy but alerted” fallback message.

Posts the AI-generated draft into Slack for double approval.
Upon approval, automatically emails the response to the customer.
